records.microscopy description: There are about 18,000 species, both marine and freshwater, in many shapes and forms. There are both branched and unbranched forms here which are transparent, colorless, flat or cylindrical filaments. They are about 1 µm wide; most are 10-50 µm long, and show first-order grays and white (001001, 001011). Rounded forms are various diameters (<l to 100+ µm); most here are 8-10 µm .
records.Extended description: Algae are unicellular or colonial aquatic plants. There are about 18,000 species, both marine and freshwater, in many shapes and forms. This sample consists of dried, powdered lake algae. There are both branched and unbranched forms here which are transparent, colorless, flat or cylindrical filaments. They are about 1 µm wide; most are 10-50 µm long, and show first-order grays and white (001001, 001011). Rounded forms are various diameters (<l to 100+ µm); most here are 8-10 µm . They are transparent, colorless, isotropic (000000), or show gray interference colors (001000). Algae include the diatoms (4) q.v. (000010, 000011, 010010, 010011). Any of the above may have colored pigment inclusions of green, blue-green, red, brown; either rounded (010000) or rod shaped (010001). In addition to the algae, this sample contains calcite (133), feldspar, quartz (183), biotite (167), clay, encysted protozoans, settled combustion products, and miscellaneous plant and animal tissue remains in various states of dehydration and decomposition.

records.microscopy description: Single cells may also be present, but one more frequently sees sheets of individual cells. The transparent, colorless to light tan sheets (001010, 011010) sometimes have one or more folds. The surface texture appears soft and scaly. When dandruff is lost, a number of these other particles come away with it. Note the birefringent paper fiber (001001).
records.Extended description: Dandruff scales are made up of epithelial cells (3), q.v. Single cells may also be present, but one more frequently sees sheets of individual cells. The transparent, colorless to light tan sheets (001010, 011010) sometimes have one or more folds. The interference colors are very weak gray, not usually more than 100 nm retardation. The surface texture appears soft and scaly. Dandruff usually contains a great variety of artifacts, especially paper and textile fibers, because oily skin acts as a dust collector. When dandruff is lost, a number of these other particles come away with it. Note the birefringent paper fiber (001001).

records.microscopy description: Skin tissue is stratified, with a basal layer of newly produced columnar cells. These pass successively outward, become flattened and are cornified by the time they reach the surface. Cells from the scalp usually flake off in sheets. They may be deeply folded on themselves or rolled up like scrolls. They are transparent, colorless or light tan, polygonal flakes (000010, 010010. the average cell diameter is 20 µm.
records.Extended description: Epithelial tissues cover the human body and line the digestive tract. The cells are of several different kinds, but the most important are from the outer human skin. Skin tissue is stratified, with a basal layer of newly produced columnar cells. These pass successively outward, become flattened and are cornified by the time they reach the surface. It is this cornified top layer that scales off as dandruff (2), q.v., or as single epithelial cells. Cells from the scalp usually flake off in sheets. Individual cells or simple groups of cells come from the fingers and other parts of the body, or from weathered dandruff. They may be deeply folded on themselves or rolled up like scrolls. They are transparent, colorless or light tan, polygonal flakes (000010, 010010. The indices are about 1.53 and the interference colors, if apparent, are low (001010, 011010; the average cell diameter is 20 µm.

records.Extended description: These are unicellular or colonial aquatic plants (algae), both recent and fossil, distinguished by the complex structure of their siliceous cell walls. There are several thousand species, both marine and freshwater. Most diatoms are best likened to tiny snuffboxes. They are made up of two parallel valves and a narrow peripheral girdle. The highly ornate and detailed markings on the valves serve as the basis for classification. Most species of diatoms show a regular array of lines or dots, actually openings through the valves. These are best shown in the SEM pictures in Volume III. These regular arrays have been used by microscopists as test objects for microscope resolution, e.g., Amphipleura pellucida, with about 120,000 lines of dots per inch (ca. 0.2 µm apart). These structures often give rise to easily perceived diffraction images in the back focal plane of the objective and often lead to "structural" colors (iridescence) like those of butterfly wings (4B). The brown color is due to Rayleigh scattering; it would not be apparent if the mounting medium (Aroclor®) were not so different in refractive index. The transparent, usually colorless, usually isotropic valves may be circular, oval, triangular, linear, crescentic or boat-shaped (000010, 000011, 010010, 010011). Heat causes diatoms to devitrify to cristobalite (138); they then show moderate interference colors (001010, 001011).

records.microscopy description: These are the same transparent, colorless, isotropic, siliceous valves of aquatic plants described under diatoms (4). These, however, have been processed for extending paint ("diatomaceous silica"), and have, accordingly, been crushed to small size. The fragments here range from < 1 µm to 10 µm; fragments over 20 µm and whole diatoms seldom survive the milling process.
records.Extended description: These are the same transparent, colorless, isotropic, siliceous valves of aquatic plants described under diatoms (4). These, however, have been processed for extending paint ("diatomaceous silica"), and have, accordingly, been crushed to small size. The fragments here range from < 1 µm to 10 µm; fragments over 20 µm and whole diatoms seldom survive the milling process. The refractive index of the frustule is 1.43 (000010, 000011). The commercial processing of diatoms may involve heat. Heat causes diatoms to devitrify to cristobalite; they then show moderate interference colors (001010, 001011).

records.microscopy description: When such areas that support the organisms dry, certain forms become encysted, others die. Encysted protozoans in this sample are in colorless, transparent, isotropic, 3-5 µm spheres (000000).
records.Extended description: Infusoria are microscopic organisms found in infusions of decayed organic matter and in stagnant water. When such areas that support the organisms dry, certain forms become encysted, others die. The resulting dried, organism-laden soil is infusorial earth. This sample is especially rich in diatoms (4) (000010, 000011) and other algae (1) (000000, 001000, 001001, 001011, 010000, 010001). The diatom valves may contain decayed cellular material giving them color (010010, 010011). Encysted protozoans in this sample are in colorless, transparent, isotropic, 3-5 µm spheres (000000). Soil minerals and other soil constituents are always found in infusorial earth. This sample is particularly rich in hematite (390) and it also contains humus.

records.microscopy description: These are the same kinds of transparent, colorless, isotropic siliceous valves of aquatic plants described under diatoms (4). These, however, act as a carrier for grain insecticide. The diatom valves in this sample are less than 1 µm to more than 50 µm .
records.Extended description: These are the same kinds of transparent, colorless, isotropic siliceous valves of aquatic plants described under diatoms (4). These, however, act as a carrier for grain insecticide. The insecticide itself is not evident in the sample and would have to be detected by chemical tests. The diatom valves in this sample are less than 1 µm to more than 50 µm . Some of the large frustules appear brown due to Rayleigh scatter (000010, 000011). When diatoms are observed microscopically in a medium having a refractive index close to that of the diatoms (ca 1.43) both the structural colors and Rayleigh scattering disappear. Some fragments are needlelike (000011, 000001).

records.microscopy description: Their colorless to yellow-brown shells are composed of gelatinous, chitinous or limy material, or of selected bits of sand, sponge spicules or other debris. They may be spheres (001000, 011000), tubes (001001, 011001), spirals or other shapes, and they frequently resemble snail shells; broken fragments are platy (001010, 011010). They are transparent to translucent but appear to be opaque if the chambers are filled with air. The surface is smooth to rough; Foraminifera range in size from 10 µm to 150 mm.
records.Extended description: Foraminifera are an order of the animal kingdom composed of some 18,000 species, recent and fossil. Most of them are marine. Their colorless to yellow-brown shells are composed of gelatinous, chitinous or limy material, or of selected bits of sand, sponge spicules or other debris. They may be spheres (001000, 011000), tubes (001001, 011001), spirals or other shapes, and they frequently resemble snail shells; broken fragments are platy (001010, 011010). They are transparent to translucent but appear to be opaque if the chambers are filled with air. The surface is smooth to rough; in many forms the shell is perforated with minute holes (see SEM micro graphs of this sample in Volume III). Foraminifera range in size from 10 µm to 150 mm. Between crossed polars, they are high-order white; many fragments show a black extinction cross similar to that seen in a uniaxial interference figure.

records.microscopy description: Insect parts are varied in shape, but if they are large enough they always show organized structure. Wings (000010, 010010, 001010, 011010) are thin, almost isotropic films which may be smooth, or covered with hairs,scales or ridges; The color may range from colorless to opaque but is usually yellow or brown.
records.Extended description: Insect parts are varied in shape, but if they are large enough they always show organized structure. Legs (010001, 011001) are jointed and may be smooth or hairy. Wings (000010, 010010, 001010, 011010) are thin, almost isotropic films which may be smooth, or covered with hairs,scales or ridges; vessels and structural elements are almost always seen. Antennae (010001, 011001) may be filamentous, bulbous or featherlike. Body parts (010000, 011000, 010010, 011010) may be smooth, hairy, scaly, perforated, figured and hard or soft. Insect parts most frequently seen are: chitinous body parts, fragments of wings and legs, isolated scales and hairs. The color may range from colorless to opaque but is usually yellow or brown. Birefringence may be moderate to low or nil. The refractive indices are nearly all about 1.54-1.55, with a few lower than this. Photomicrograph 9A shows principally leg and body parts; 9B shows a large wing fragment covered with short, pointed hairs.

records.microscopy description: Moth and butterfly scales are very thin, transparent to translucent, isotropic films, resembling in outline snow-shoes, surfboards, teardrops, fans, duck feet or arrowheads (000010, 010010, 000011, 010011). The free edge may be plain, rounded, scalloped or picket-fencelike; The scales are colorless to shades of gray or tan when viewed microscopically by transmitted light.
records.Extended description: Moth and butterfly scales are very thin, transparent to translucent, isotropic films, resembling in outline snow-shoes, surfboards, teardrops, fans, duck feet or arrowheads (000010, 010010, 000011, 010011). The short "stem" is the point of attachment to the wing. The free edge may be plain, rounded, scalloped or picket-fencelike; scent scales have a tufted edge. Close longitudinal striations mark the surface (about 55 lines per 100 µm in this sample), and at high magnification pigment particles are evident. The SEM micrographs in Volume III show these ordered striations very well. It is these that cause the iridescent colors of butterfly and moth wings. In longitudinal cross section, the scale is seen to taper at the free edge. The scales are colorless to shades of gray or tan when viewed microscopically by transmitted light.

records.microscopy description: american elm pollen (ulmus aericana).These transparent to translucent, pale yellow grains look like collapsed spheres when mounted in nonaqueous media. The surface of the grain suggests the convolutions of the human brain. In aqueous media (11 B), the grains swell to spheres about 40 µm in diameter (28-55 µm); they are slightly polygonal in polar view. The wall thickness is 1.5-3 µm .
records.Extended description: These transparent to translucent, pale yellow grains look like collapsed spheres when mounted in nonaqueous media. (11 A). The surface of the grain suggests the convolutions of the human brain. In aqueous media (11 B), the grains swell to spheres about 40 µm in diameter (28-55 µm); they are slightly polygonal in polar view. The wall thickness is 1.5-3 µm . There are usually 5 pores but there may be 3-7 arranged around the equator. The exine is thickened around the pores. The stain in llB is fuchsin. The descriptive characteristics of pollens used for identification are: The extent to which pollens and spores usually shrink in Aroclor® and other nonaqueous media is shown for each pollen (11-23). In each case, the pollen in the A photomicrographs is mounted in Aroclor® and in the B photomicrographs in an aqueous medium containing fuchsin.

records.microscopy description: cottonwood pollen (populus deltoides).Figure 12A shows the grains mounted in Aroclor®, a nonaqueous medium; the transparent, isotropic grains look like wads of wrinkled paper about 22 µm in diameter. In an aqueous staining medium, such as acid fuchsin in polyvinyl alcohol and lactic acid (12B), the colorless (000000) to pale yellowish (010000) grains expand and are uneven to perfectly spheroid. There are no pores, and the surface is finely granular. The grains are 25-30 µm in diameter; the exine is almost 4 µm thick.
records.Extended description: This is an allergenic tree pollen. Figure 12A shows the grains mounted in Aroclor®, a nonaqueous medium; the transparent, isotropic grains look like wads of wrinkled paper about 22 µm in diameter. In an aqueous staining medium, such as acid fuchsin in polyvinyl alcohol and lactic acid (12B), the colorless (000000) to pale yellowish (010000) grains expand and are uneven to perfectly spheroid. There are no pores, and the surface is finely granular. The grains are 25-30 µm in diameter; the exine is almost 4 µm thick. The extent to which pollens and spores usually shrink and become malformed is obvious in these and the following figures (13-23).

records.microscopy description: dandelion pollen (taraxacum officinale).These grains are extremely variable in size (12-29 µm X 13-30 µm); normally they are about 25 µm (12-50 µm) in diameter. About half of the grains are abnormal and deviate from the basic form, i.e., they are asymmetric and deformed. The granular surface of the irregular, tetraradiate grains is marked by crests and ridges. The ridges are 4-5 µm high. Spines 2.5 µm long and about 2.5 µm apart cover the surface.
records.Extended description: These grains are extremely variable in size (12-29 µm X 13-30 µm); normally they are about 25 µm (12-50 µm) in diameter. About half of the grains are abnormal and deviate from the basic form, i.e., they are asymmetric and deformed. The granular surface of the irregular, tetraradiate grains is marked by crests and ridges. The ridges are 4-5 µm high. Spines 2.5 µm long and about 2.5 µm apart cover the surface. There are as many as 15 depressions (4-6 in abnormal), 3 containing about 8 µm diameter pores. The exine is on the thick side. The stain in 13B is fuchsin.

records.microscopy description: horse-chestnut pollen (aesculus hippocastanum).In Aroclor® or other nonaqueous mounting media (14A) these grains are football-shaped 25 µm X 14 µm . The grains fold at the three furrows. In aqueous media, the grains are spherical and about 35 µm in diameter. A membrane can be seen to protrude from the pores-generally 1-3 µm above the circular profile. Careful focusing will show numerous (12-60) small (< 1 µm) projections studding the pore membrane. The surface is smooth to very finely granular.

records.microscopy description: lamb's-quarters pollen.An allergenic weed pollen, lamb's-quarters looks, in non-aqueous media, like roughened spheres with a wavy outline; many of the transparent, isotropic grains are collapsed on one side (15A). In aqueous media, the light yellow, spheroidal grains (15B) are 25.8 µm across (21.3-28.9 µm). Fifty to seventy pores cover the smooth surface. The pores are 1.5 µm in diameter and about 3.0 µm apart.

records.microscopy description: sugar maple pollen (acer saccharum).In nonaqueous media,transparent to translucent, isotropic grains are oblate spheroids and look like prunes or footballs with one or two deep folds (16A). In aqueous media, the tannish grains are rounded triangles (16B). Three furrows taper to sharp ends at the poles. The granular skin, or exine, is about 3 µm thick and the diameteris about 35 µm.

records.microscopy description: marihuana (hemp) pollen (cannabis sativa).In Aroclor® or other nonaqueous mounting media, these grains are generally football to collapsed football shaped, about 26 µ.m X 14 µ.m. In aqueous media they are generally irregular spheroidal, 21-25 µ.m diameter; The surface is smooth to very finely granular. There are thickenings on the inside cell wall that extend deeply into the grain.

records.microscopy description: red oak pollen (quercus rubra).In nonaqueous media, the transparent to translucent, isotropic grains are roughly rectangular with round comers, and deep folds parallel to the longer sides (18A). In aqueous media, the pale yellow, oblately flattened grains resemble rounded equilateral triangles (18B). The relatively rigid exine is about 3 µ.m thick and the average diameter is 34 µm.
records.Extended description: This is an allergenic tree pollen. In nonaqueous media, the transparent to translucent, isotropic grains are roughly rectangular with round comers, and deep folds parallel to the longer sides (18A). In aqueous media, the pale yellow, oblately flattened grains resemble rounded equilateral triangles (18B). The three furrows and three pores are prominent. The bulges at the apices are the germ pores. The relatively rigid exine is about 3 µ.m thick and the average diameter is 34 µm. The grains in IBB have been stained with acid fuchsin.

records.microscopy description: pine pollen (pinus sp).This transparent to translucent pollen has an oval body with two attached bladders. The pale to light yellow body is a rounded to oblate ellipsoid. The surface markings are coarsely reticulated and granular. The surface pattern is much like that on the cap, but somewhat enlarged. These grains, observed in an aqueous medium (20B), are 22 X 40 µm exclusive of bladders; with bladders, the particles average 40 X 75 µm (40 X 60-90 µm).

The bladders are attached to the margins of the cap. The surface pattern is much like that on the cap, but somewhat enlarged. These grains, observed in an aqueous medium (20B), are 22 X 40 µm exclusive of bladders; with bladders, the particles average 40 X 75 µm (40 X 60-90 µm). There may be one encircling bladder or as many as four bladders, depending on the species of tree. The stain in 20B is acid fuchsin.

In aqueous media (21B), the regular to uneven spheres are 20-24 µm in diameter (but may be as high as 35 µm). The surface texture is grainy with no furrows or pores. The cell wall is about 2.5 µm thick.

records.microscopy description: ragweed pollen (ambrosia sp).It is isotropic, generally spherical (oblate spheroidal) and covered with short spines. The transparent to translucent grains average 18.0 X 19.3 µm (16.2-20.4 X 17.9-21.3 µm). The pale yellow skin, or exine, has a granular surface. The spines are about 0.5 µ.m high and about 1.7-3.4 µm apart. The grains have three furrows 4.5 X 1.6 µ.m and three elliptical pores 4.0 X 1.6 µm, one in each furrow. The grains are apt to show one or two depressions when mounted in Aroclor®;
records.Extended description: This allergenic pollen is probably the one most frequently reported in pollen count surveys. It is isotropic, generally spherical (oblate spheroidal) and covered with short spines. The transparent to translucent grains average 18.0 X 19.3 µm (16.2-20.4 X 17.9-21.3 µm). The pale yellow skin, or exine, has a granular surface. The spines are about 0.5 µ.m high and about 1.7-3.4 µm apart. The grains have three furrows 4.5 X 1.6 µ.m and three elliptical pores 4.0 X 1.6 µm, one in each furrow. This sample is mounted both in a nonaqueous medium (22A) and in an aqueous medium (22B). The grains are apt to show one or two depressions when mounted in Aroclor®; this gives them a pinched effect. The grains in 22B have been stained with acid fuchsin.

records.microscopy description: timothy grass pollen (phleum pratense).In resinous, nonaqueous media, the transparent, colorless to extremely pale yellow timothy grass pollen looks like collapsed spheres presenting a roughly triangular or tetrahedral view (23A). In aqueous media, the isotropic pollen swells to spheres 32 µm (26.4-30.0 µm) in diameter (23B). There is one circular 3.4 µm pore, with a central 1.6 µm lid (operculum). The outside skin, or exine, is 2 µm thick and raised around the pore. The surface is finely granular.

records.microscopy description: The colorless, porous skeleton is honeycom blike; perforations may appear circular, oval or hexagonal. The horny or siliceous skeleton is composed of spicules which may unite to form structures resembling baskets, beehives or turbans. The structures are frequently spired and/ or on supporting "legs." Other forms are like twisted pretzels or schematic radiating suns. Radiolarians range in size from a few micrometers to several centimeters; these average 125 µm across;
records.Extended description: Radiolaria are an order of unicellular animals. Their transparent to translucent outer skeletons, illustrated here, are usually composed of isotropic silica (000000, 000010) but sometimes of anisotropic strontium sulfate (001000, 001010). The colorless, porous skeleton is honeycom blike; perforations may appear circular, oval or hexagonal. The horny or siliceous skeleton is composed of spicules which may unite to form structures resembling baskets, beehives or turbans. The structures are frequently spired and/ or on supporting "legs." Other forms are like twisted pretzels or schematic radiating suns. Radiolarians range in size from a few micrometers to several centimeters; these average 125 µm across; fragments are common. Radiolaria are exclusively marine. Both fossil and recent forms occur. The radiolaria in this sample are isotropic.

records.microscopy description: Transparent, colorless to yellow, scaly, curly fibers with low birefringence are typical of Spanish moss, an air plant, or epiphyte, that grows on either dead or live trees and even on telephone poles and wires. Individual scales resemble peacock feathers, seashell patterns or fish scales (001010, 011010) and have irregular, fan- to flame-shaped fibrils radiating from an "eye." They are 150-200 µm wide, 500-750 µm long and very thin. The surface is smooth to rough and irregular.
records.Extended description: Transparent, colorless to yellow, scaly, curly fibers with low birefringence are typical of Spanish moss, an air plant, or epiphyte, that grows on either dead or live trees and even on telephone poles and wires. Individual scales resemble peacock feathers, seashell patterns or fish scales (001010, 011010) and have irregular, fan- to flame-shaped fibrils radiating from an "eye." They are 150-200 µm wide, 500-750 µm long and very thin. The surface is smooth to rough and irregular. Bundles of fibers are common. Spanish moss is found chiefly in swamps, from Florida to Texas and Mexico, and north on the Atlantic coastal plain to eastern Virginia. It is used for stuffing mattresses and upholstered furniture.

records.microscopy description: Transparent, colorless, isotropic "pine needles." These are slightly curved, smooth, siliceous cylinders, averaging 6.5 µm wide and 150 µm long. Transparent, colorless, calcareous spicules.
records.Extended description: Spicules, the "skeletons" of sponges, are of many different kinds, sizes and shapes. Spicules from two representative species of the more than 3000 appear in this sample: 1. Transparent, colorless, isotropic "pine needles." These are slightly curved, smooth, siliceous cylinders, averaging 6.5 µm wide and 150 µm long. The refractive index is about 1.47 (000001). 2. Transparent, colorless, calcareous spicules. These smooth, three- or four-branched or forked, or even single rods, with bright first-, second- and even third-order interference colors are calcite (133) (001001). The refractive indices of calcite are 1.658 (CtJ) and 1.486 (e); (-) 0.171.

records.microscopy description: spore. fern spores -three species. The largest particles (40-70 µm), which have taken the acid fuchsin stain only slightly, are from the cinnamon fern (Osmunda cinnamonea). They are translucent, pale yellow to light yellow-green, distorted spheres, footballs and tetrads, or nearly globular; there is a faintly marked Y-shaped crest on the scurfy rough surface (010000). The surface projections are 1-2 µm high and 2-3 µm apart. The medium-size particles are from the marginal shield fem, Dryopteris marginalis. These yellow-brown, translucent spores average 40 X 25 µm and have not taken the stain (010000).
records.Extended description: Fem spores, unlike pollens, generally have heavy walls and either stain poorly or do not take a stain at all with, for example, acid fuchsin (27B). They are usually marked by crests which indicate the areas that were in contact with the other three spores during formation of the tetrad; these crests help to distinguish fem spores from pollens. This sample contains three species of windborne fern spores mounted in Aroclor® (27 A) and in aqueous poly-vinyl alcohol (27B). 1. The largest particles (40-70 µm), which have taken the acid fuchsin stain only slightly, are from the cinnamon fern (Osmunda cinnamonea). They are translucent, pale yellow to light yellow-green, distorted spheres, footballs and tetrads, or nearly globular; there is a faintly marked Y-shaped crest on the scurfy rough surface (010000). The surface projections are 1-2 µm high and 2-3 µm apart. 2. The medium-size particles are from the marginal shield fem, Dryopteris marginalis. These yellow-brown, translucent spores average 40 X 25 µm and have not taken the stain (010000). They appear semilunar or like an orange slice. The surface is covered with coarse, discontin-uous ridges and bumps 1-4 µm high, giving a deeply figured appearance. 3. The smallest particles, also unstained, are from the rattlesnake fern, Botrychium virginianum. The transparent, colorless spores are generally spherical, averaging 25 µm across (18-30 µm) (000000). Closely spaced wartlike projections are about 3 µm in diameter and 1-2 µm high; there is also a Y-crest on the surface. In general, fern spores may be colorless or colored but all are isotropic with refractive indices near 1.53.

records.microscopy description: spore. alternaria. The shape is suggestive of insect pupae or rattle-snake rattles -see fungal conidia (32). They are brown when fresh, isotropic and about 30 µm long (7-72 µm). Terminal conidia are "beaked," and the specialized hyphal branches (conidiophores) are tubelike, simple or branched, and segmented. The pale yellow to brown isotropic segments are variable in length but here are about 7 µm wide and 15 µm long;
records.Extended description: septa. The shape is suggestive of insect pupae or rattle-snake rattles -see fungal conidia (32). They are brown when fresh, isotropic and about 30 µm long (7-72 µm). Terminal conidia are "beaked," and the specialized hyphal branches (conidiophores) are tubelike, simple or branched, and segmented. The pale yellow to brown isotropic segments are variable in length but here are about 7 µm wide and 15 µm long; many are ballooned. This widespread fungus is an important cause of hayfever.

records.microscopy description: spore. aspergillus. The colorless to brown isotropic spores in this sample of Aspergillus niger are about 3.6 µmin diameter and appear as collapsed spheres in resinous media (000000, 010000). They swell to about 9-10 µm in diameter and 5 µm in breadth. The spores are found in compact, spherical or columnar sporeheads. The conidiophores (specialized hyphae) are hyaline or colored, flat or rounded, about 10-12 µm in diameter, birefringent (gray) and characterized by a "foot" formed at the point where they arise from the hypha (001001, 011001, 001011, 011011).
records.Extended description: The colorless to brown isotropic spores in this sample of Aspergillus niger are about 3.6 µmin diameter and appear as collapsed spheres in resinous media (000000, 010000). In aqueous media, the spores appear like pulley-wheels a disc with convex faces. They swell to about 9-10 µm in diameter and 5 µm in breadth. The spores are found in compact, spherical or columnar sporeheads. The conidiophores (specialized hyphae) are hyaline or colored, flat or rounded, about 10-12 µm in diameter, birefringent (gray) and characterized by a "foot" formed at the point where they arise from the hypha (001001, 011001, 001011, 011011). The stalk may expand into a sac with one or two projections (sterigmata). Aspergillus has the ability to produce alcohol, enzymes, fats, acids, antibiotics and toxins; they are important in human and animal diseases.

records.microscopy description: spore. penicillium. The spores in this sample of Penicillium notatum are colorless to very pale yellow, isotropic, rounded to ellipsoidal and appear dimpled in resinous media (000000, 010000). The transparent hyphae are 5 µm in diameter, septate, branched, birefringent (grays) and colorless 001001, 001011).
records.Extended description: The spores in this sample of Penicillium notatum are colorless to very pale yellow, isotropic, rounded to ellipsoidal and appear dimpled in resinous media (000000, 010000). The transparent hyphae are 5 µm in diameter, septate, branched, birefringent (grays) and colorless 001001, 001011). Penicillium is characterized by spore chains growing on the fingerlike tufted penicillus (pencils) at the ends of the conidiophores. In bulk, the mold is green; it is seen on stale bread, cheese, rotting fruit etc.

records.microscopy description: spore. wheat smut spores. In nonaqueous media such as Aroclor®, the translucent, isotropic, light to dark brown, rimmed discs usually look like little "seeds" or oval cups, averaging 4.5 µm in diameter. In aqueous media, they swell, lose their cup shape and look like rimmed discs with a slightly distorted circumference; many are oval or egg-shaped. They average 6.75 µm across in aqueous media. The surface is smooth.
records.Extended description: These are typical of fungus (mold) spores. In nonaqueous media such as Aroclor®, the translucent, isotropic, light to dark brown, rimmed discs usually look like little "seeds" or oval cups, averaging 4.5 µm in diameter. In aqueous media, they swell, lose their cup shape and look like rimmed discs with a slightly distorted circumference; many are oval or egg-shaped. They average 6.75 µm across in aqueous media. The surface is smooth.

records.microscopy description: spore. fungus (conidia). Many fungi form a mass of cottony growth, or mold, known as a mycelium. The segmented and branched, tubelike conidiophores in this sample are about 5 µm wide; the walls occur about every 7-8 µm ; The conidio-phores are transparent, colorless to medium brown and isotropic (000001, 010001). Fungal conidia shown here are transparent to translucent, light yellow to dark brown, isotropic, approximately oval to clavate structures which are usually walled to form 2 to 8 chambers. These are 5-20 µm wide and 12-40 µm long (010000).
records.Extended description: Many fungi form a mass of cottony growth, or mold, known as a mycelium. It is made up of individual fibers, or hyphae, which may be segmented and/ or twisted. A specialized hyphal branch-a conidiophore-produces successive conidia, usually by abstriction. The conidia are asexual spores which ultimately develop new hyphae. The segmented and branched, tubelike conidiophores in this sample are about 5 µm wide; the walls occur about every 7-8 µm ; many segments appear ballooned. The conidio-phores are transparent, colorless to medium brown and isotropic (000001, 010001). Fungal conidia shown here are transparent to translucent, light yellow to dark brown, isotropic, approximately oval to clavate structures which are usually walled to form 2 to 8 chambers. The conidia are suggestive of insect pupae or rattlesnake rattles. These are 5-20 µm wide and 12-40 µm long (010000).

records.microscopy description: spore. mold (fungus). The sporangiophores are transparent, colorless, isotropic, smooth cylinders or twisted ribbons, 10-12 µm wide (000001, 000011). The spores are transparent, colorless, isotropic, smooth, oval bodies, 3-5 µm across (000000). The spore heads, about 40 µm across, are covered with spores. When all of these have been discharged, the barren head is seen to be almost spherical or mushroom-shaped. It is transparent, orange and isotropic (010000).
records.Extended description: This mold from pecans is included as typical of many sporulating molds. The cottony masses (mycelium) usually thought of as mold are made up of individual fibers, or hyphae, of three kinds. Some (stolons) grow horizontally; these send others (rhizoids) into the substratum; other hyphae (sporangiophores) grow upright. The ends of the sporangiophores develop enlarged spore heads, each bearing hundreds of asexual spores. The sporangiophores are transparent, colorless, isotropic, smooth cylinders or twisted ribbons, 10-12 µm wide (000001, 000011). The spores are transparent, colorless, isotropic, smooth, oval bodies, 3-5 µm across (000000). The spore heads, about 40 µm across, are covered with spores. When all of these have been discharged, the barren head is seen to be almost spherical or mushroom-shaped. It is transparent, orange and isotropic (010000).

records.microscopy description: spore. shaggy ink cap (coprinus comatus). The spores of the inky-cap mushrooms are transparent, dark brown, subspherical to elliptical, 5-7 µm by 5-12 µm. The walls of these isotropic spores are thick (to 2.5 µm). There is a thin-walled pore at one end of the spore, with a diameter of about 2.5 µm.
records.Extended description: The spores of the inky-cap mushrooms are transparent, dark brown, subspherical to elliptical, 5-7 µm by 5-12 µm. The walls of these isotropic spores are thick (to 2.5 µm). There is a thin-walled pore at one end of the spore, with a diameter of about 2.5 µm.

records.microscopy description: spore. mushroom spores (agaricus campestris). The translucent, isotropic spores of this common field mushroom, shown mounted in Aroclor®, are broadly ovoid or almond-shaped. The spores average 5 X 6.5 µm; the apiculus, when present, is about 1 µm long. The spore surface is smooth, and the color ranges from light tan to purple-brown.
records.Extended description: The translucent, isotropic spores of this common field mushroom, shown mounted in Aroclor®, are broadly ovoid or almond-shaped. They may show a basal apiculus, or point of attachment. The spores average 5 X 6.5 µm; the apiculus, when present, is about 1 µm long. The spore surface is smooth, and the color ranges from light tan to purple-brown.

records.microscopy description: spore. puffball (scleroderma aurantium). The transparent, isotropic, yellowish-brown spores in this sample are spherical and 3--4 µm in diameter (010000). In aqueous media, the spores swell to about 10 µm in diameter. The surface of the spore is covered with numerous tiny spines, but these are difficult to see with the light microscope when the untreated spores are in resinous media. The filaments in the sample are brownish, transparent cylinders or collapsed cylinders.
records.Extended description: The transparent, isotropic, yellowish-brown spores in this sample are spherical and 3--4 µm in diameter (010000). They appear darker here because of entrapped air. In aqueous media, the spores swell to about 10 µm in diameter. The surface of the spore is covered with numerous tiny spines, but these are difficult to see with the light microscope when the untreated spores are in resinous media. The filaments in the sample are brownish, transparent cylinders or collapsed cylinders. The weak birefringence may be masked in very dark fibers (011001, 011011).

records.microscopy description: spore. moss spores (funaria sp). These spores, mounted in Aroclor® 5442, are variously shaped, collapsed and distorted spheres; Surface depressions may produce a coarsely wrinkled appearance. The transparent to translucent isotropic spores are lime-green and average 12 µm across (6-15 µm); some grains, perhaps older, are yellow. The surface is coarsely granular. In aqueous media, the grains swell somewhat and resemble slightly distorted spheres and ovals.
records.Extended description: These spores, mounted in Aroclor® 5442, are variously shaped, collapsed and distorted spheres; they may appear hemispherical and puckered in one, two or three places. Some resemble collapsed tetrads. Surface depressions may produce a coarsely wrinkled appearance. The transparent to translucent isotropic spores are lime-green and average 12 µm across (6-15 µm); some grains, perhaps older, are yellow. The surface is coarsely granular. In aqueous media, the grains swell somewhat and resemble slightly distorted spheres and ovals.

records.microscopy description: spore. lycopodium spores. Each spore is a transparent to translucent, pale yellow, three-sided pyramid with a rounded base in the form of a quarter-sphere; as a matter of fact, this is the way the spore forms. A Y-crest on the surface marks the formal association in the tetrad. The spores are about 31 X 38 µm averaging roughly 35 µm . They are isotropic and do not take the stains commonly used for pollen. The surface is covered with a layer of transparent cells.
records.Extended description: These are spores of a club moss, a family of plants related to the fems. Each spore is a transparent to translucent, pale yellow, three-sided pyramid with a rounded base in the form of a quarter-sphere; as a matter of fact, this is the way the spore forms. A Y-crest on the surface marks the formal association in the tetrad. The spores are about 31 X 38 µm averaging roughly 35 µm . They are isotropic and do not take the stains commonly used for pollen. The surface is covered with a layer of transparent cells. In focus, the surface of this layer looks like a honeycomb of cells, or a raised, ridged network of cell walls. Exuded oil droplets are frequently seen.

records.microscopy description: These transparent, scaly cylinders taper to a point at the free end. They are 1-1.5 cm long and up to 50+ µm in diameter, lthough the diameter tends to vary somewhat along the same hair shaft. There are 8-11 fairly prominent, overlapping scales per 100 µm, forming a distinct pattern. The medulla is mostly absent, but when it appears it shows as irregularly placed, dark, oval pockets of air 3-6 µm X 6-10 µm.
records.Extended description: These transparent, scaly cylinders taper to a point at the free end. They are 1-1.5 cm long and up to 50+ µm in diameter, lthough the diameter tends to vary somewhat along the same hair shaft. Some of the guard hairs are unpigmented (001001), but the hairs of the undercoat are rather heavily pigmented light to dark brown, and red-dish brown (011001). There are 8-11 fairly prominent, overlapping scales per 100 µm, forming a distinct pattern. The medulla is mostly absent, but when it appears it shows as irregularly placed, dark, oval pockets of air 3-6 µm X 6-10 µm. Interference colors are moderate first-order. Extinction is parallel. The refractive indices are about 1.55 (lengthwise and about 1.54 (crosswise); (+) 0.01.

records.microscopy description: These transparent, colorless, scaly cylinders are bulbous at the point of attachment, narrow near the base, thicker toward the middle and tapered to a point at the free end (001001). (a) Waved mosaic 25-35 µm wide on hairs with 4-6 scales per 100 µm. (b) Close crenate (having a scalloped margin) on hairs with 12 scales per 100 µm. These hairs are 65 µm (50-70 µm) wide. (c) Waved crenate on hairs with 25 scales per 100 µm. These hairs are 75-80 µm wide.
records.Extended description: These transparent, colorless, scaly cylinders are bulbous at the point of attachment, narrow near the base, thicker toward the middle and tapered to a point at the free end (001001). At least four kinds of scale patterns occur. (a) Waved mosaic 25-35 µm wide on hairs with 4-6 scales per 100 µm. (b) Close crenate (having a scalloped margin) on hairs with 12 scales per 100 µm. These hairs are 65 µm (50-70 µm) wide. (c) Waved crenate on hairs with 25 scales per 100 µm. These hairs are 75-80 µm wide. (d) Mosaic on hairs with 9-10 scales per 100 µm. These hairs are 60 µm wide. Another outstanding characteristic of cat hair is the medulla, which appears opaque when filled with air. It is a ladderlike row of patches (uniserial) suggestive of a string of beads; it may also be simple and unbroken. Some hairs may be pigmented (011001). Extinction is parallel and nearly complete. The refractive indices are about 1.54 (crosswise) and about 1.55 (lengthwise); (+) 0.01. Interference colors in this sample are first-order.

records.microscopy description: These colorless (001011) to pale yellowish-brown (011011), transparent fibers are long continuous ribbons. They are 15-30 µm wide and about 3 µm thick. Abnormalities, including thickenings, occur at irregular intervals along the length, as well as flattened cross-over points as in silk, cultivated (56). Longitudinal striations are due to fibrils less than 0.5 µm to 1 µm diameter, which are colorless, transparent continuous cylinders (001001). The fibrils are held together in the fiber by a weakly birefringent mucilage. Apparent cross striations 5-10 µm apart at places along the fiber are actually cracks and breaks in this mucilage.
records.Extended description: These colorless (001011) to pale yellowish-brown (011011), transparent fibers are long continuous ribbons. They are 15-30 µm wide and about 3 µm thick. Abnormalities, including thickenings, occur at irregular intervals along the length, as well as flattened cross-over points as in silk, cultivated (56). Longitudinal striations are due to fibrils less than 0.5 µm to 1 µm diameter, which are colorless, transparent continuous cylinders (001001). These are best seen at frayed ends. Extinction of the fibrils is parallel and complete. The interference colors are moderate first-order, mostly white and grays, although some portions show up to second-order blue. The refractive indices are about 1.54 (crosswise) and 1.59 (lengthwise); (+) 0.05. The fibrils are held together in the fiber by a weakly birefringent mucilage. Apparent cross striations 5-10 µm apart at places along the fiber are actually cracks and breaks in this mucilage. In this sample, the mucilage, while still wet, has picked up a variety of soil and airborne particles, including iron oxides and combustion products.

records.microscopy description: The transparent fibers have nodes at intervals of about five to ten times their diameter. The width in this sample averages 5 µm (3-10 µm) ; the length averages 1200 µm (380-1800 µm). Bits of broken quill may be flat (001010, 011010).
records.Extended description: Nearly all feathers are smooth stems with attached parallel barbs (001001, 011001). The transparent fibers have nodes at intervals of about five to ten times their diameter. The width in this sample averages 5 µm (3-10 µm) ; the length averages 1200 µm (380-1800 µm). Chickens (as well as other fowl) have three principal kinds of feathers: 1. Contour feathers (pennae). These have a stiff shaft and firm vane. 2. Down feathers (plumulae). These have a soft shaft and vane. On some down feathers there is no shaft the barbs arise from the end of the quill. 3. Pinfeathers (filoplumulae). These are slender shafts with few or no barbs. Many feather shafts have booklets on one side which hold adjacent barbs together. Extinction is parallel and complete. The sign of elongation is positive and the interference colors are low first-order. The refractive indices are about 1.55. Bits of broken quill may be flat (001010, 011010).

records.microscopy description: These transparent, colorless, scaly cylinders are bulbous at the point of attachment, and taper at the free end (001001). The finely toothed scales, about 12 per 100 µm, form an irregular mosaic pattern. Hair length is about 1-5 cm; the diameter varies widely, 12-180 µm, although commercial carpet samples average 36 µm. In this sample, the medulla is about ½o the diameter of the hair. This is a low-grade fiber used for coarse carpet
records.Extended description: These transparent, colorless, scaly cylinders are bulbous at the point of attachment, and taper at the free end (001001). The finely toothed scales, about 12 per 100 µm, form an irregular mosaic pattern. Hair length is about 1-5 cm; the diameter varies widely, 12-180 µm, although commercial carpet samples average 36 µm. The cortex is finely striated. Pigmentation varies from unpigmented white to brown, black and red (011001). A large proportion of the hairs are unmedullated. When the medulla does appear, it is single rowed and relatively narrow; sometimes slitlike. In this sample, the medulla is about ½o the diameter of the hair. Extinction is parallel. The refractive indices are about 1.54 (crosswise) and about 1.55 (lengthwise); (+) 0.01. Interference colors in this sample go to third-order red. Hairs from the tail and from calf fibers have different characteristics. This is a low-grade fiber used for coarse carpet

records.microscopy description: These transparent to translucent, scaly, cylindrical hairs from a small dog, a chihuahau, taper to a rounded point at the free end (001001). The smooth-edged scales, 10-12 per 100 µm, form a regular mosaic. The medulla, which occupies 50-80% of the fiber width, may look opaque due to trapped air bubbles. The fibers in this sample are unpigmented and 10-90 µm in diameter.
records.Extended description: These transparent to translucent, scaly, cylindrical hairs from a small dog, a chihuahau, taper to a rounded point at the free end (001001). The smooth-edged scales, 10-12 per 100 µm, form a regular mosaic. The fibers may contain brown, black or red pigment (011001). The central canal, or medulla, when present, is simple and unbroken though it may be fragmental near the free end. The medulla, which occupies 50-80% of the fiber width, may look opaque due to trapped air bubbles. The fibers in this sample are unpigmented and 10-90 µm in diameter. Some variation in characteristics can be expected with different breeds. Extinction is parallel and nearly complete. The interference colors are mostly first-order with indices about 1.54 (crosswise) and 1.55 (lengthwise);(+) 0.01.

records.microscopy description: These transparent to translucent, scaly, cylindrical hairs are from a large dog-the German shepard. The identifying characteristics are identical to those of the previous dog hair (small) (44), except that the width of these fibers is, in general, narrower (10-75 µm) than for the smaller dog.
records.Extended description: These transparent to translucent, scaly, cylindrical hairs are from a large dog-the German shepard. The identifying characteristics are identical to those of the previous dog hair (small) (44), except that the width of these fibers is, in general, narrower (10-75 µm) than for the smaller dog. Also, the distribution of brown pigment is much greater in these hairs.

records.microscopy description: The scales here are 18-22 µm long, so that there are 5-6 scales per 100 µm. The hairs themselves are transparent and colorless, tapering to a point at the free end. The fibers are 10-90 µm wide. Average widths for the commercial fiber are: kid, 25 µm; first quality, 30 µm; second quality, 44 µm;
records.Extended description: The scales here are 18-22 µm long, so that there are 5-6 scales per 100 µm. They are only faintly visible and hardly overlap, forming an irregular, waved mosaic pattern. They lie so close to the stem that it appears smooth. The hairs themselves are transparent and colorless, tapering to a point at the free end. A central canal, or medulla, may be evident. Pigment may also be present, but the brownish hue of some gross samples in the raw state is due to the fact that as much as 30% is sand, various dusts and grease. The best commercial grades are clear white. The fibers are 10-90 µm wide. Average widths for the commercial fiber are: kid, 25 µm; first quality, 30 µm; second quality, 44 µm; third quality, 56 µm. Extinction is parallel and nearly complete. The refractive indices are 1.54 (crosswise) and 1.55(lengthwise)(+) 0.01.

records.microscopy description: The scale length and projection of the tip are visible in the fiber outline. There are 10-12 scales per 100 µm (4-9 per 100 µm in fine wools). Scales are 8-18 µm long. The true wool hairs are 10-70 µmin diameter. Sheep have two distinct fiber types: the outer fibers (guard hairs) and the fine, crimpy true wool of the undercoat seen in this sample. Especially coarse, brittle and strongly medullated guard hairs (kemp fibers) are 70-200 µm in diameter.
records.Extended description: Prominent, overlapping scales cover these transparent, colorless cylinders in a definite pattern (see especially SEM 47, Volume III). The scale length and projection of the tip are visible in the fiber outline. Physical properties vary greatly. There are 10-12 scales per 100 µm (4-9 per 100 µm in fine wools). The edges are serrated and wavy in coarse wools. In the best qualities, the medulla is absent; when present it may be fragmented, interrupted or continuous. Scales are 8-18 µm long. The true wool hairs are 10-70 µmin diameter. Sheep have two distinct fiber types: the outer fibers (guard hairs) and the fine, crimpy true wool of the undercoat seen in this sample. Especially coarse, brittle and strongly medullated guard hairs (kemp fibers) are 70-200 µm in diameter. Extinction is parallel and nearly complete. The refractive indices are 1.556 (lengthwise) and 1.547 (crosswise); (+) 0.009.

records.microscopy description: These transparent to translucent, scaly cylinders taper to a rounded point at the free end (001001). Mane hair is highly circular, 50-200 µm (average 125 µm) in width and the medulla is wide and latticelike. The scales form a smoothed, close-toothed edge, with 9-12 scales per 100 µm.
records.Extended description: These transparent to translucent, scaly cylinders taper to a rounded point at the free end (001001). Mane hair is highly circular, 50-200 µm (average 125 µm) in width and the medulla is wide and latticelike. The concentration of pigment granules is greatest near the outer boundary of the medulla and least dense toward the scaly cuticle (011001). Cross sections of the tips of these hairs show a narrow medulla. The pigment is again mostly at the boundary of the medulla, but now forms radial projections toward the cuticle. The scales form a smoothed, close-toothed edge, with 9-12 scales per 100 µm. The extinction is parallel and incomplete. The interference colors are second-order with indices about 1.54 (crosswise) and 1.55 (lengthwise); (+) 0.01.

records.microscopy description: Human hairs may be transparent to almost opaque, with circular or oval cross sections (001001, 011001). The cuticle is usually six to eight scale layers thick and covers the entire fiber. The central canal, or medulla, which is opaque if filled with air, may be as much as one third the width of the hair and may be continuous, fragmented or absent. Human hair ranges from 50 to 150 µm in diameter. Animal hairs are usually less than half the diameter of the finest human hair although the guard hairs are more than twice that of the coarsest human hair. Extinction between crossed polars is usually regular and parallel along the length of the hair, but from some parts of the body, hairs are more irregular in cross section (bumpy) and lack uniform extinction ("polycrystalline").
records.Extended description: Human hairs may be transparent to almost opaque, with circular or oval cross sections (001001, 011001). The scalloped, overlapping scales do not protrude from the shaft very much. The cuticle is usually six to eight scale layers thick and covers the entire fiber. The central canal, or medulla, which is opaque if filled with air, may be as much as one third the width of the hair and may be continuous, fragmented or absent. Medullae of larger hairs tend to be more continuous. Pigments may be absent to considerable. Human hair ranges from 50 to 150 µm in diameter. Animal hairs are usually less than half the diameter of the finest human hair although the guard hairs are more than twice that of the coarsest human hair. Human hair types vary, depending on age, race, sex and the portion of the body concerned. The indices are about 1.542 (crosswise) and 1.554 (lengthwise); (+) 0.012. Extinction between crossed polars is usually regular and parallel along the length of the hair, but from some parts of the body, hairs are more irregular in cross section (bumpy) and lack uniform extinction ("polycrystalline"). The mean range of density of non-medullated hairs is about 1.335 to 1.348 g/cm3.

records.microscopy description: The electric razor is indicated by the short (70-130 µm) lengths of hair cut at an angle of about 30° (20-45°). Thin, fibrous fragments may appear to be isotropic because of the low birefringence of hair.
records.Extended description: The identifying characteristics of the hair in this sample are identical to those described above (49) ; the identifying characteristics of the skin cells are those described under epithelial cells (3). The electric razor is indicated by the short (70-130 µm) lengths of hair cut at an angle of about 30° (20-45°). The cut ends are not particularly clean and may be quite jagged. Hairs shaved in opposite directions on successive days result in trapezoidal fragments. Thin, fibrous fragments may appear to be isotropic because of the low birefringence of hair. Hairs cut with safety razors show smoother, clean-cut ends, including some which are concave. There are also a greater variety of cutting angles shown. About 20% of this electric razor sample consists of skin cells. Finally, hair samples from safety razors consist of about 50% skin cells (000010, 010010).

records.microscopy description: Because of a more elliptical cross section, there is a greater tendency for the hair of Blacks to show apparent variation in fiber diameter. Fibers in this sample are 40-125 µm wide.
records.Extended description: The identifying characteristics of these fibers are similar to those described under human hair (Caucasian) (49). No sharp demarcations exist between human hairs, but here the pigment granules are very much increased in number and form elongated aggregates. In pigmented human hair, there is a tendency for the granules to be more densely concentrated in the cortex nearer to the cuticle; the area immediately around the medulla is more lightly pigmented or devoid of granules. Also, melanine granules are larger in Blacks' hair than in Caucasian or Oriental. Because of a more elliptical cross section, there is a greater tendency for the hair of Blacks to show apparent variation in fiber diameter. Fibers in this sample are 40-125 µm wide. Variation in scale pattern is also to be expected. In cross section, this sample would show a 1-2 layered cuticle at the ends of the minor axis and a 6-8 layered cuticle at the ends of the major axis.

records.microscopy description: Inspection along the entire fiber length and of cross sections shows a very uniform and constant almost circular diameter along the same shaft and between hairs. The hairs in this sample are uniformly 90 µm.
records.Extended description: The identifying characteristics of these fibers are similar to those described under human hair (Caucasian) (49). The pigment granules are very much increased in number and form elongated aggregates, though to a lesser extent than in the previous sample (51). In pigmented human hair, there is a tendency for the granules to be more densely concentrated in the cortex nearer to the cuticle; the area immediately around the medulla is more lightly or not pigmented. Inspection along the entire fiber length and of cross sections shows a very uniform and constant almost circular diameter along the same shaft and between hairs. The hairs in this sample are uniformly 90 µm. Variation in scale pattern is to be expected.

records.microscopy description: Two types of hair can be distinguished here: in the outer, heavier guard hairs (over 100 µm wide), the scale pattern is a slightly interrupted, waved mosaic; In the finer fur fiber, which averages 13.5 µm in diameter (5-30 µm), the scale pattern fluctuates toward the tip between single and double chevron (001001, 011001).
records.Extended description: Two types of hair can be distinguished here: in the outer, heavier guard hairs (over 100 µm wide), the scale pattern is a slightly interrupted, waved mosaic; the margins are almost smooth. Toward the middle of each scale, the pattern is double chevron, and at the tip it is single chevron. In the finer fur fiber, which averages 13.5 µm in diameter (5-30 µm), the scale pattern fluctuates toward the tip between single and double chevron (001001, 011001). Pigments may be present in the body, or cortex, of the fibers, but never at the extreme free ends. The central canal, or medulla, is characteristically a ladderlike chain of patches suggestive of a string of pearls (uniserial); two or more rows are not uncommon (biserial and multiserial). The extinction is parallel and very nearly complete. Indices are about 1.54 (crosswise) and 1.55 (lengthwise). The interference colors are low first-order except in the guard hairs where they may be slightly higher.

records.microscopy description: These transparent, scaly cylinders taper at the free end (001001). The scales are large, prominent and form a sharp-toothed edge. There are 3-7 scales per 100 µm. each medullary section is constricted to form a block "T." In guard hairs, there are multiple-rowed medullas-2-4 rows of segments in the mouse and up to 10 rows in the rat. There are usually 1-4 places along the hair where the diameter decreases sharply; The hairs in this sample are 4-60 µm wide.
records.Extended description: These transparent, scaly cylinders taper at the free end (001001). The scales are large, prominent and form a sharp-toothed edge. There are 3-7 scales per 100 µm. The medulla consists of blocklike segments; each medullary section is constricted to form a block "T." In guard hairs, there are multiple-rowed medullas-2-4 rows of segments in the mouse and up to 10 rows in the rat. The medulla may appear black due to entrapped air. Pigment, when present, is usually at one end of the medullary segment; the other end is clear. The spherical pigment granules are rather large and compact, especially in the mouse. Granules seldom appear in the cortex, but when they do, they are black or dark brown and are distributed equally on both sides of the medulla. There are usually 1-4 places along the hair where the diameter decreases sharply; these help to distinguish rat hairs from cat hairs. The hairs in this sample are 4-60 µm wide. Extinction is parallel. The refractive indices are about 1.54 (crosswise) and 1.55 (lengthwise); (+) 0.01. Interference colors are low first-order.

records.microscopy description: These pale yellow to yellow-brown, transparent fibers look like broad, continuous ribbons (001011, 011011), but they are actually thin wedge-shapes in cross section. The width of the fiber averages 35 µm although it varies considerably along the length. Longitudinal striations are due to fibrils 0.3-1.5 µm wide which make up the fiber.
records.Extended description: These pale yellow to yellow-brown, transparent fibers look like broad, continuous ribbons (001011, 011011), but they are actually thin wedge-shapes in cross section. The width of the fiber averages 35 µm although it varies considerably along the length. Longitudinal striations are due to fibrils 0.3-1.5 µm wide which make up the fiber. Some of the smooth fibers are twisted. Extinction is parallel and incomplete. The interference colors are moderate first-order, and the refractive indices are about 1.54 (crosswise) and 1.59 (lengthwise).

records.microscopy description: Although these transparent, colorless fibers appear to be smooth, continuous cylinders of almost constant diameter, cross sections reveal that most are rounded-polygonal. The fibers show transverse or oblique depressions at intervals, resulting partly from reeling operations and partly from fiber crossings on the cocoon. The latter may appear doubled because silk, as it comes from the "spinneret," is a double fiber, i.e., two fibers (have) held parallel by gum. The diameter is usually 10-12 µm (25 µm maximum).
records.Extended description: Although these transparent, colorless fibers appear to be smooth, continuous cylinders of almost constant diameter, cross sections reveal that most are rounded-polygonal. The fibers show transverse or oblique depressions at intervals, resulting partly from reeling operations and partly from fiber crossings on the cocoon. The latter may appear doubled because silk, as it comes from the "spinneret," is a double fiber, i.e., two fibers (have) held parallel by gum. Reeling, carried out under hot water, dissolves this gum and separates the fibers. The photomicrograph shows threadlike bundles of silk fibers. The characteristics of individual fibers including cross-over marks are shown on one or two single fibers. The diameter is usually 10-12 µm (25 µm maximum). Extinction is parallel and nearly complete. The refractive indices are 1.591 (lengthwise) and 1.538 (crosswise); (+) 0.053.

records.microscopy description: These transparent, scale-covered cylinders are 7-100 µm in diameter. The scales are fairly prominent and number about 9 per 100 µm for the thicker, outer hair. The granules are disposed in streaks parallel to the length.
records.Extended description: These transparent, scale-covered cylinders are 7-100 µm in diameter. The scales are fairly prominent and number about 9 per 100 µm for the thicker, outer hair. The medulla is semicompartmentalized. In thick hairs, it is continuous and about half as wide as the entire hair. In finer hairs, it is continuous to fragmented and about one-quarter as wide as the entire hair. The pigment granules are dark brown. They are densely concentrated near the medulla; the area near the cuticle is clear. The granules are disposed in streaks parallel to the length. Extinction is complete. Large fibers show second-order colors; narrow fibers show first-order colors. Indices are about 1.54 (crosswise) and 1.55 (lengthwise); (+) 0.01.

records.microscopy description: These colorless, transparent, continuous, smooth-surfaced cylinders may be seen as individual or paired filaments. The filament is generally round in cross section but occasionally is flattened or otherwise distorted and may show an undulating edge. The filaments here are I. 7 µm wide, but about 5% are only 1 µm wide.
records.Extended description: These colorless, transparent, continuous, smooth-surfaced cylinders may be seen as individual or paired filaments. When paired, they are sometimes fused. The filament is generally round in cross section but occasionally is flattened or otherwise distorted and may show an undulating edge. The filaments here are I. 7 µm wide, but about 5% are only 1 µm wide. Extinction is parallel and complete. Low first-order colors. The birefringence is about 0.01 (+).

records.microscopy description: These are transparent, colorless tubes (001001) which have collapsed into irregularly to regularly twisted ribbons (001011). the tip is a tapered rod. The irregularly smooth surface has occasional transverse markings. The fibers are 8-33 µm wide and 17 mm (10-27.2 mm) long. The length and quality of the fibers vary, depending on the source and maturity. In cross section, these seed fibers are linear to circular;
records.Extended description: These are transparent, colorless tubes (001001) which have collapsed into irregularly to regularly twisted ribbons (001011). The point of attachment is conical to cylindrical; the tip is a tapered rod. There is a central canal, although both this lumen and the convolutions are absent from the tip regions. The irregularly smooth surface has occasional transverse markings. The fibers are 8-33 µm wide and 17 mm (10-27.2 mm) long. The length and quality of the fibers vary, depending on the source and maturity. In cross section, these seed fibers are linear to circular; the more circular the cross section, the smaller the lumen. A notable identifying characteristic is the lack of extinction (due to spiraling cells) between crossed polars. The indices are 1.578 (lengthwise) and 1.532 (crosswise); (+) 0.046.

records.microscopy description: The result is a transparent, colorless, almost cylindrical fiber with a small to fragmented lumen. In this sample, the fibers average 10 µm in width (8-12 µm).
records.Extended description: Mercerization is a process for treating cotton yarn or cloth, sometimes under tension, with alkali (caustic soda). It makes the material lustrous, strong and receptive to dyes. Convolutions and lumen almost completely disappear. The result is a transparent, colorless, almost cylindrical fiber with a small to fragmented lumen. Some fibers retain their convolutions, which aid in their identification. In this sample, the fibers average 10 µm in width (8-12 µm). They do not show extinction, but they may show decreased intensity when they are parallel to the polars. The indices of fibers mercerized under tension are 1.566 (lengthwise), 1.522 (crosswise); (+) 0.044; without tension they are 1.544 (lengthwise), 1.524 crosswise); (+) 0.030. See cotton (59) for other characteristics.

records.microscopy description: Linters are colorless to buff, transparent, fuzzy, short fibers that adhere to the cottonseed after ginning. They are distinguished from other cotton fibers by their irregular width and short length; they are especially characterized by shape abnormalities, including crooks, hooks, wartlike growths and a variety of other distortions. The fibers in this sample are 17 µm wide (10-25 µm) and may be up to 7 mm long.
records.Extended description: Linters are colorless to buff, transparent, fuzzy, short fibers that adhere to the cottonseed after ginning. They are flattened, ribbonlike tubes with a central canal. They are distinguished from other cotton fibers by their irregular width and short length; they are especially characterized by shape abnormalities, including crooks, hooks, wartlike growths and a variety of other distortions. The fibers in this sample are 17 µm wide (10-25 µm) and may be up to 7 mm long. Interference colors are first-order and low second-order. See cotton (59) for other characteristics.

records.microscopy description: The transparent, colorless to extremely pale yellow fibers are 7 µm (4-11 µm) wide and 1.5 mm (0.5-2.5 mm) long. The chief distinguishing characteristic of esparto grass is the presence of small teardrop-shaped cells, or "commas," which are from hooked hairs on the surface of the leaf (001001). They may appear as branching hairs from the surface, or they may be isolated. These "commas" are 8 µm (5-12 µm) at the greatest width and 30 µm (25-40 µm) long.
records.Extended description: Esparto grass fibers are long, slender, irregular tapering cylinders (001001). The lumen is narrow. The transparent, colorless to extremely pale yellow fibers are 7 µm (4-11 µm) wide and 1.5 mm (0.5-2.5 mm) long. Serrated epidermal cells (001011) are usually numerous. The chief distinguishing characteristic of esparto grass is the presence of small teardrop-shaped cells, or "commas," which are from hooked hairs on the surface of the leaf (001001). They may appear as branching hairs from the surface, or they may be isolated. These "commas" are 8 µm (5-12 µm) at the greatest width and 30 µm (25-40 µm) long. The fibers do not show extinction. The birefringence is moderate; fibers in this sample show gray, white and first-order yellow interference colors. The figure shows the long tapering fibers and several of the characteristic "commas." Fine flaxlike nodes (63) can also be seen.

records.microscopy description: These colorless to pale yellow bast fibers are straight, smooth and rounded-polygonal in cross section (001001, 011001). The individual fibers in this sample are transparent and are about 11 µm wide, although the average width of flax in general is closer to 17 µm; in length, the fibers can reach 3.0 cm. In cross section, mature fibers are oval to polygonal; immature fibers tend to be irregularly oval with a larger lumen.
records.Extended description: These colorless to pale yellow bast fibers are straight, smooth and rounded-polygonal in cross section (001001, 011001). Slight thickenings at transverse nodes in shapes like I's, X's, V's and Y's are most readily observed between crossed polars. The individual fibers in this sample are transparent and are about 11 µm wide, although the average width of flax in general is closer to 17 µm; in length, the fibers can reach 3.0 cm. Translucent bundles of 2 to 10 fibers are common. The fibers have a very narrow, indistinct lumen. In cross section, mature fibers are oval to polygonal; immature fibers tend to be irregularly oval with a larger lumen. The indices are 1.594 (lengthwise) and 1.532 (crosswise); (+) 0.062. Extinction is parallel for single fibers, but bundles may show none; it is incomplete at the nodes. Linen is made up of flax fibers.

records.microscopy description: These bast fibers are transparent, colorless cylinders with surface irregularities such as joints, fractures and swollen tissue. Individual fibers average 22 µm (10-50 µm) in width and may be from a few millimeters to several centimeters in length. The smooth fibers are polygonal in cross section with rounded edges. The lumen is broad and flat, becoming small at the end of the fiber. The indices are 1.585-1.591 (length-wise) and 1.526-1.530 (crosswise); There are many varieties of hemp including manila and sisal but the true hemp (Cannabis sativa) is the principal rope- and bag-making fiber.
records.Extended description: These bast fibers are transparent, colorless cylinders with surface irregularities such as joints, fractures and swollen tissue. Bundles are not uncommon. Individual fibers average 22 µm (10-50 µm) in width and may be from a few millimeters to several centimeters in length. The smooth fibers are polygonal in cross section with rounded edges. The lumen is broad and flat, becoming small at the end of the fiber. Irregularly shaped cell ends are blunt and may show lateral branching. Star-shaped crystals of calcium oxalate (486) may be present (001000). The bundles and individual fibers show parallel extinction except at the nodes. The indices are 1.585-1.591 (length-wise) and 1.526-1.530 (crosswise); (+) 0.06. There are many varieties of hemp including manila and sisal but the true hemp (Cannabis sativa) is the principal rope- and bag-making fiber.

records.microscopy description: These are transparent, colorless to pale yellow, generally straight, smooth cylinders (001001, 011001) with occasional cross markings (nodes). Both ends of the fiber taper to points. Individual fibers average 20 µm (15-25 µm) in width and are 200 µm to 8 mm in length. These bast fibers are most likely to be seen in bundles, since jute is usually used in bast form and seldom sepa-rated down to the individual fibers. In cross section, the fibers are polygonal with sharply defined angles. The figure shows mostly fiber bundles.
records.Extended description: These are transparent, colorless to pale yellow, generally straight, smooth cylinders (001001, 011001) with occasional cross markings (nodes). The cell walls are thick and large; the lumen is irregular with constrictions. Both ends of the fiber taper to points. Individual fibers average 20 µm (15-25 µm) in width and are 200 µm to 8 mm in length. These bast fibers are most likely to be seen in bundles, since jute is usually used in bast form and seldom sepa-rated down to the individual fibers. In cross section, the fibers are polygonal with sharply defined angles. The bundles and fibers show parallel extinction except at the nodes. The refractive indices are 1.577 (lengthwise) and 1.536 (crosswise); (+) 0.041. The figure shows mostly fiber bundles. Jute is exceeded in world production only by cotton.

records.microscopy description: They are transparent, colorless, smooth, hollow, thin-walled cylinders, frequently seen bent over themselves.
records.Extended description: These fibers of Bombax malabarica are from India. They are transparent, colorless, smooth, hollow, thin-walled cylinders, frequently seen bent over themselves. The fibers, which are sometimes flattened (001011) are unicellular hairs which grow on the inner wall of the pods which constitute the fruit. The fibers taper to a point at the free end, and at the other end have a slightly bulbous base with annular or reticulate markings. The length is 2-3 cm, and the diameter is 10-35 µm, Chemically, the fibers are 61-64% cellulose; much of the remainder is lignin. The specific gravity of the air-filled cylinders is about 0.055. Extinction is parallel. Interference colors are low first-order.

records.microscopy description: Mature ramie fibers are transparent, colorless and approximately cylindrical (001001). The immature fibers have some twist, and the tips are rounded. They are 40 µm (25-80 µm) wide and average 14 cm (6-65 cm) in length. This is the longest single plant fiber cell known. Except at the nodes, its surface is smooth and extinction is parallel. The indices are 1.596 (length-wise) and 1.528 (crosswise) ;
records.Extended description: Mature ramie fibers are transparent, colorless and approximately cylindrical (001001). They have nodelike ridges and longitudinal striations, and no twist. The cell wall is thick, and the lumen is well defined. Immature ramie fibers are flattened, ribbonlike cylinders (001011). The immature fibers have some twist, and the tips are rounded. They are 40 µm (25-80 µm) wide and average 14 cm (6-65 cm) in length. This is the longest single plant fiber cell known. Except at the nodes, its surface is smooth and extinction is parallel. The indices are 1.596 (length-wise) and 1.528 (crosswise) ; (+) 0. 068. Immature fibers, being thinner, show lower-order interference colors.

records.microscopy description: Sisal fibers are transparent, colorless to light yellowish tan and approximately cylindrical with characteristic broadening toward the middle (001001, 011001). In cross section, these leaf fibers are polygonal. The fibers are 20-32 µm wide and 1.5-4.0 mm long. Numerous short, thick-walled fiber cells with a narrow lumen and surface pores are common. Other cells lack surface markings. Commercial sisal fibers are used in the form of strands or bundles of individual fibers.
records.Extended description: Sisal fibers are transparent, colorless to light yellowish tan and approximately cylindrical with characteristic broadening toward the middle (001001, 011001). The ends are usually thick and blunt, sometimes pointed and occasionally even forked. In cross section, these leaf fibers are polygonal. The cell walls are thick and the lumen, though large, is not prominent. The fibers are 20-32 µm wide and 1.5-4.0 mm long. Numerous short, thick-walled fiber cells with a narrow lumen and surface pores are common. Other cells lack surface markings. Occasionally one will find spiral vessels and tissue cells containing calcium oxalate (486) crystals; 1.49 (a) to 1.65 ('y); (+) 0.16 (001000). Commercial sisal fibers are used in the form of strands or bundles of individual fibers. The fibers do not show extinction.

records.microscopy description: Wheat straw consists of several kinds of birefringent particles having indices around 1.53. The four major types of particles are: 1. Transparent, colorless to yellow, thick-walled, somewhat tapering fibers, 13 µm (7-24 µm) wide and 1.5 mm (0.7-3.1 mm)long. Extinction is parallel except at occasional surface cross markings (001001, 011001). Transparent, colorless to pale yellow fibers with thin smooth walls and almost pointed ends. These are 27-34 µm wide and 0.8-2.9 mm long (001001, 011001).
records.Extended description: Wheat straw consists of several kinds of birefringent particles having indices around 1.53. The four major types of particles are: 1. Transparent, colorless to yellow, thick-walled, somewhat tapering fibers, 13 µm (7-24 µm) wide and 1.5 mm (0.7-3.1 mm)long. Extinction is parallel except at occasional surface cross markings (001001, 011001). 2. Transparent, colorless to pale yellow fibers with thin smooth walls and almost pointed ends. These are 27-34 µm wide and 0.8-2.9 mm long (001001, 011001). 3. Large, transparent, almost colorless, thin-walled, parenchymatous, or "baggy," cells are long oval to rounded- rectangular. Almost isotropic, they are about 40-80 µm wide and 250 µm long (001010, 011010). 4. Serrated epidermal cells are colorless to yellow, transparent cells about 15 X 50 µm. The walls are deeply serrated; cells are joined in the plant walls like interlocking pieces of a jigsaw puzzle (001001, 011001).

records.microscopy description: In most samples, these transparent, colorless to light yellow fibers will have originated from paper or paper products. Whole tapered fibers are 20-27 µm wide and 0.75-1.14 mm long.
records.Extended description: In most samples, these transparent, colorless to light yellow fibers will have originated from paper or paper products. This sample is distinguished as nonconiferous, or hardwood, by the large baggy cells or vessel elements (001010, 001011) with sometimes as many as ten rows of pits and by Hat, tapering fibers without pits (001010). Mechanical treatment is indicated by the ripped and tomfibers and by the irregular fragments and bundles of ligninrich fibers (011001, 011011). Especially characteristic of mechanical pulping operations are the medullary rays crossing other fibers at right angles. This sample is aspen (Populus tremuloides). Whole tapered fibers are 20-27 µm wide and 0.75-1.14 mm long. The pitting of these vessels is characteristically alternate. The large baggy cells show undulose extinction.
