records.microscopy description: These opaque, black, equant fragments of ferrite are rounded to irregular in both edge and outline. Their surfaces are granular and they are strongly magnetic (100000). This ferrite is an iron which, in steel or pig iron, has not combined with carbon to form the carbide cementite. It exists in several forms which vary both in magnetism and in ability to dissolve cementite.
records.Extended description: These opaque, black, equant fragments of ferrite are rounded to irregular in both edge and outline. Their surfaces are granular and they are strongly magnetic (100000). Many of the particles are lightly to heavily coated with transparent, red-orange, rounded particles of the iron oxide, hematite (223,390,391) (011100). This ferrite is an iron which, in steel or pig iron, has not combined with carbon to form the carbide cementite. It exists in several forms which vary both in magnetism and in ability to dissolve cementite.

records.microscopy description: There are some transparent, brownish, isotropic spheres with index greater than 1. 66 (010100) , and some which are opaque, brown-ish, rounded particles (110000). Agglomerates up to 20 µm are common although a few opaque, rounded particles may be up to 40 µm.
records.Extended description: Ferrochrome is a 'high-chromium iron alloy used for adding chromium to iron and steel. This sample is the electric furnace emission of the ferrochrome process. The oxide particles shown here are mostly 1 µm (>0.5-4 µm), transparent and colorless, yellowish, orange-brown and brown, isotropic, rounded or spherical particles with a refractive index less than 1.66 (000000, 010000). There are some transparent, brownish, isotropic spheres with index greater than 1. 66 (010100) , and some which are opaque, brown-ish, rounded particles (110000). Agglomerates up to 20 µm are common although a few opaque, rounded particles may be up to 40 µm. There is no magnetic component.

records.microscopy description: ferromagnesium dust | Opaque, rounded, compact particles with smooth to moderately coarse outlines and finely granular surfaces. These nonmagnetic particles constitute about 90% of the sample. Opaque, black, coarsely jagged fragments of magnetic iron (165) (100000).
records.Extended description: This dust from the dustcatcher of a ferromagnesium plant consists of: 1. Opaque, rounded, compact particles with smooth to moderately coarse outlines and finely granular surfaces. Most are dark gray to black, but many have an earthy brown or pinkish cast (100000). These nonmagnetic particles constitute about 90% of the sample. 2. Opaque, black, coarsely jagged fragments of magnetic iron (165) (100000). They are about 6% of the sample. 3. Transparent, deep red fragments of hematite (390) (011100). These comprise about 2% of the sample.

records.microscopy description: ferromagnesium dust | Opaque, rounded, compact particles with smooth to moderately coarse outlines and finely granular surfaces. These nonmagnetic particles constitute about 90% of the sample. Opaque, black, coarsely jagged fragments of magnetic iron (165) (100000).

records.microscopy description: ferrosilicon dust | Transparent, colorless, isotropic silica smoke which probably consists of individual particles less than a hundred nanometers in diameter. The aggregates are rounded, 35 µm in diameter. Slivers and equant fragments of black, opaque, hard coal (559) (100000).
records.Extended description: Obtained from a ferrosilicon furnace, this dust consists of: 1. Transparent, colorless, isotropic silica smoke which probably consists of individual particles less than a hundred nanometers in diameter. The aggregates are rounded, 35 µm in diameter. The refractive index is about 1.45. Approximately 95% of the sample is represented here (000000). 2. Slivers and equant fragments of black, opaque, hard coal (559) (100000). These comprise about 5% of the sample.

records.microscopy description: foundry dust | Opaque, black, sharp-edged, equant fragments of magnetic iron (392) (100000).
records.Extended description: This sample from a molding sand cleaning system has five components: 4. Opaque, black, sharp-edged, equant fragments of magnetic iron (392) (100000). 5. Transparent, rounded, deep red particles of iron oxide (223, 390,391); the indices are 2.94 (epsilon) to 3.22 (omega); (-) 0.28 (011100).

records.microscopy description: The particles are transparent, colorless, isotropic, rounded, 0.5 µm and less in diameter, with a refractive index of about 1.
records.Extended description: This dust is a fume from a gold smelter. It is composed of 94% arsenic trioxide. The particles are transparent, colorless, isotropic, rounded, 0.5 µm and less in diameter, with a refractive index of about 1. 755. The hardness is 1.5, and the specific gravity is 3.87. A few percent of finely divided hematite (390, 391) and silica are also present.

records.microscopy description: Opaque, black, sharply angular flakes of graphite make up about 90% of the sample. Their surfaces are smooth. Some are in layered agglomerates, occasionally showing rounded 120Â° angles and even forming rounded hexagonal tablets. The excellent reflectivity from the small flakes and agglomerates (100010) is apparent when they are oriented properly.
records.Extended description: Three major components appear here: 1. Opaque, black, sharply angular flakes of graphite make up about 90% of the sample. Their surfaces are smooth. Some are in layered agglomerates, occasionally showing rounded 120Â° angles and even forming rounded hexagonal tablets. The excellent reflectivity from the small flakes and agglomerates (100010) is apparent when they are oriented properly. 2. Opaque, black, rather coarse, equant fragments of magnetic Fe3O4 (165, 407) (100000). These constitute about 5% of the sample; many are covered with hematite (390). 3. Transparent, deep red, rounded particles of iron oxide (223, 391) (011100). They are about 5% of the sample. Traces of quartz (183) (001000) and calcite (133) (001000) can also be found in this sample.

records.microscopy description: Rounded to irregularly shaped, magnetic particles up to 150 µm in diameter of iron (392) or steel (100000).
records.Extended description: Actually, there are three components in this sample: 1. Rounded to irregularly shaped, magnetic particles up to 150 µm in diameter of iron (392) or steel (100000). About 20%. 2. Less than 0.5 µm to 2 µm, rounded to elongated, equant particles of hematite, Fe2O3 [see the following description of iron oxide (391) for the optical properties of hematite; see also jewelers' rouge, (223)] (011100). About 40%. 3. Individual rounded particles and plates, <1-150 µm, of goethite, HFeO2. See limonite (162) for the optical properties of goethite (011100, 011110). About 40%.

records.microscopy description: The simple agglomerates are opaque and red-orange in top light. Individual grains are transparent and blood-red with (omega) brownish red and (epsilon) yellowish red.
records.Extended description: These are rounded to elongated, equant grains (2 µm in average diameter) of Fe20 3 , hematite. The simple agglomerates are opaque and red-orange in top light. Individual grains are transparent and blood-red with (omega) brownish red and (epsilon) yellowish red. The indices range from 2.95, Li (omega) to 2.74 (epsilon); (-) 0.21. They have also been reported to be 3.01, Li (omega) to 2.78 (epsilon); (-) 0.23. The hardness is 5; the density, 5.2; the melting point, 1350°C. Hematite is soluble in HCl and is nonmagnetic.

records.microscopy description: About 95% of the sample is made up of opaque, gunmetal gray to black, equant particles of iron, Fe, with sharp, jagged edges (100000). Others are rounded; some are nearly spheres. All have grainy surfaces and are magnetic.
records.Extended description: This sample has two components: 1. About 95% of the sample is made up of opaque, gunmetal gray to black, equant particles of iron, Fe, with sharp, jagged edges (100000). Others are rounded; some are nearly spheres. All have grainy surfaces and are magnetic. The specific gravity is 7.86. 2. Transparent, deep red, smooth, equant fragments of Fe2O3, hematite (390, 391). These constitute about 5% of the sample (011100).

records.microscopy description: Opaque, dark gray to black, rounded, equant particles of iron (392). Magnetic, rough in outline and coarsely granular, they constitute about 98% of the sample (100000). This oxideis almost invariably associated with iron particles especially if they have been exposed to the atmosphere for longer than a day or two.
records.Extended description: The two components of this sample are: 1. Opaque, dark gray to black, rounded, equant particles of iron (392). The light spots in the photomicrograph are due to top lighting, not transmission. Magnetic, rough in outline and coarsely granular, they constitute about 98% of the sample (100000). 2. Transparent, blood-red, equant fragments of Fe2O3, hematite (390) (011100). They make up about 2% of the sample. This oxideis almost invariably associated with iron particles especially if they have been exposed to the atmosphere for longer than a day or two.

records.microscopy description: Opaque, dark gray, rounded and elongated, equant fragments of cast iron. These magnetic particles are rough in outline; many of the surfaces show parallel striations (100000). These particles constitute about 98% of the sample.
records.Extended description: Two components make up this sample: 1. Opaque, dark gray, rounded and elongated, equant fragments of cast iron. These magnetic particles are rough in outline; many of the surfaces show parallel striations (100000). These particles constitute about 98% of the sample. 2. Transparent, deep red fragments of Fe2O3, hematite (390) (011100). They are about 2% of the sample.

records.microscopy description: These opaque, smooth metal spheres are less than 2-5 µm in diameter. The "bright center" of each spherical particle is due to top lighting and not to light transmission. If a magnet is moved close to such a sample, the spheres tend to be mutually attracted and line themselves up in the direction of the magnetic force like parallel strings of beads. the particle size is usually 3-20 µm.
records.Extended description: These opaque, smooth metal spheres are less than 2-5 µm in diameter. The "bright center" of each spherical particle is due to top lighting and not to light transmission. If a magnet is moved close to such a sample, the spheres tend to be mutually attracted and line themselves up in the direction of the magnetic force like parallel strings of beads. Carbonyl iron is formed by decomposing (with heat) iron carbonyl vapor. The final iron powder is 99.6-99.9% pure iron; the particle size is usually 3-20 µm. Carbonyl iron is used in magnetic fluids, catalysts, pharmaceuticals, powder metallurgy and the high-frequency cores used in electronics.

records.microscopy description: iron ore roasting dust | Some of the rounded, equant particles are steel gray to black (crystals), or red en masse; they are opaque except in thin, deep red to red-orange fragments. In these thin flakes, omega is brownish red and epsilon is yellowish red (011100, 011110).
records.Extended description: Three components make up this sample: 1. Fe2O3, hematite (390). This is 95% of the sample. Some of the rounded, equant particles are steel gray to black (crystals), or red en masse; they are opaque except in thin, deep red to red-orange fragments. In these thin flakes, omega is brownish red and epsilon is yellowish red (011100, 011110). 2. Opaque, black, rough, strongly magnetic fragments of magnetite (165) (100000); about 5% of this sample.

records.microscopy description: Opaque, gray to black, coarse, spongy iron fragments that resemble grape clusters and a few spheres (100000). Both fragments and spheres are magnetic.
records.Extended description: This sample's constituents are: I. Opaque, gray to black, coarse, spongy iron fragments that resemble grape clusters and a few spheres (100000). Both fragments and spheres are magnetic. They make up about 90% of the sample. Many of these spongy iron fragments completely or partially cover the quartz grains (183) (001000) which comprise about 8% of the sample. 2. Transparent, deep red particles of hematite (390) (011100), much of it coating the particles of iron. They are about 2% of the sample.

records.microscopy description: The particles are mostly 0.5-1 µm (<0.5-2 µm), transparent, colorless, rounded, apparently isotropic, with refractive indices around 2.6.
records.Extended description: This dust is an oxide fume from storage-battery lead processing. The particles are mostly 0.5-1 µm (<0.5-2 µm), transparent, colorless, rounded, apparently isotropic, with refractive indices around 2.6. Cf. massicot (406), a lead oxide.

records.microscopy description: lead blast furnace dust | (2) yellow, rounded particles of massicot (406) (011100) ;
records.Extended description: A sample of this sort contains many different kinds of particles, including a range of lead oxides, quartz, limestone, iron pyrites, iron-lime-silicate slag, arsenic compounds and a host of other compounds containing metals associated with lead ores (000000, 001000, 100000). The major constituents are (1) light red-orange to red fragments of litharge with indices 2.665 (omega) to 2.535 (epsilon); (-) 0.13 (011100); (2) yellow, rounded particles of massicot (406) (011100) ; (3) red, birefringent, equant fragments of Pb3O4 (011100). The mean index is 2.42 (Li); (-). Also, a variety of vitreous iron-lime-silicate slag particles; these can have almost any color (yellow, green to brown) and the indices range from about 1.51 to more than 1.70.

records.microscopy description: These opaque, generally elongated, rounded globules of metal are the color of tarnished silver under top light. The surfaces are smooth grainy. This kind of resemblance requires the electron or ion microprobe for identification of single particles.
records.Extended description: These opaque, generally elongated, rounded globules of metal are the color of tarnished silver under top light. The surfaces are smooth grainy. Compare with bismuth-cadmium alloy spray (363). This kind of resemblance requires the electron or ion microprobe for identification of single particles.

records.microscopy description: lime kiln dust | Colorless, isotropic, vitreous flakes with air bubble inclusions and bubbly indentations. The surfaces may be mooth or reticulated. Gray, isotropic, vitreous, flintlike flakes (in form only) with an index of less than 1.60. Opaque aggregates of tiny granules only 1-2 µm across. They resemble coke particles superficially (495) (100000). An orange (by top light), granular substance, both free and coating component 2.
records.Extended description: The four constituents that appear here are: 1. Colorless, isotropic, vitreous flakes with air bubble inclusions and bubbly indentations. The surfaces may be mooth or reticulated. The refractive indices are usually slightly less than that of Aroclor® 5442, but they show a 2. Gray, isotropic, vitreous, flintlike flakes (in form only) with an index of less than 1.60. Some have many occluded gas bubbles and appear white or gray by top light; others without gas bubbles are black by top light (010010). A few of the gray flakes show weak magnetism, indicating magnetite or iron inclusions. 3. Opaque aggregates of tiny granules only 1-2 µm across. Each granule is shiny by top light. The aggregates can be crushed by pressing on the cover slip. They resemble coke particles superficially (495) (100000). 4. An orange (by top light), granular substance, both free and coating component 2. No single particles of this trace component could be found sufficiently transparent to show a relative index or other identifying characteristics.

records.microscopy description: The 0.5-3 µm, rounded limestone particles form numerous agglomerates up to 50 µm.
records.Extended description: This dust from a lime kiln was originally calcium oxide (lime) formed by heating limestone in a kiln to about 1000°F to burn off the carbon dioxide. The resulting lime has altered back to calcium carbonate in this sample. The 0.5-3 µm, rounded limestone particles form numerous agglomerates up to 50 µm. See calcite (133) and limestone (161) for optical properties.

records.microscopy description: The limestone particles here are <0.5-25 µm, generally rounded, and form frequent agglomerates to 75 µm (001000). Flyash: 8-10% of the sample consists of flyash, including transparent and opaque 8-35 µm spheres, both colored and colorless. The limestone particles here are <0.5-25 µm, generally rounded, and form frequent agglomerates to 75 µm (001000). Cf. lime (403), and see calcite (133) and limestone (161) for optical properties. 2. Flyash: 8-10% of the sample consists of flyash, including transparent and opaque 8-35 µm spheres, both colored and colorless. records.microscopy description: Magnesite accounts for only about 2% of the sample, being present as 40 µm agglomerates of 1 µm particles (001100). 10-70 µm, rounded, colorless, transparent, isotropic particles with a refractive index greater than 1.66. Transparent, colorless, isotropic, equant, slaglike, 0.5-40 µm particles with a refractive index less than 1.66 (000000).
records.Extended description: This sample is the effluent from a drier for a magnesite processing plant just before the collector stage. Actually, there is very little magnesite in the sample. There are fourcomponents: 1. Magnesite accounts for only about 2% of the sample, being present as 40 µm agglomerates of 1 µm particles (001100). See magnesite (164) for the optical properties. 2. Sharply angular, comminuted quartz (183) up to 40 µm is present to about 18% (001000). 3. 10-70 µm, rounded, colorless, transparent, isotropic particles with a refractive index greater than 1.66. These may be individual or appear fused in botryoidal groups of two to eight (000100). About 40%. 4. Transparent, colorless, isotropic, equant, slaglike, 0.5-40 µm particles with a refractive index less than 1.66 (000000).

records.microscopy description: It consists of transparent, pale yellow (except for particles less than 2 µm across, which are almost colorless), rounded particles resembling vaguely crumbly rolled dough; other particles bear markings suggestive of brain convolutions.
records.Extended description: This sample from a metals refining company is a furnace product. It consists of transparent, pale yellow (except for particles less than 2 µm across, which are almost colorless), rounded particles resembling vaguely crumbly rolled dough; other particles bear markings suggestive of brain convolutions. In top light, the sample is milky yellow. The indices are 2.51 (alpha) to 2.71 (gamma); 0.20 (Li). Hardness is 2; density is 9.56. The particles are soluble in HN03.

records.microscopy description: Mill scale is composed of opaque flakes with irregular, sharply jagged outlines and granular surfaces (100010). Some of the surfaces show parallel wrinkles suggestive of tree bark on the air side; the side originally in contact with the metal surface is smoother. Very small particles are equant (100000).
records.Extended description: Mill scale is composed of opaque flakes with irregular, sharply jagged outlines and granular surfaces (100010). Some of the surfaces show parallel wrinkles suggestive of tree bark on the air side; the side originally in contact with the metal surface is smoother. Very small particles are equant (100000). X-ray diffraction data for these strongly magnetic particles reveal that FeO is present as well as Fe3O4. They are, of course, magnetic.

This sample is from a sand-clay mixture ready to be moistened and used in making molds for metal castings. The transparent, colorless, rounded grains are quartz (183); its indices are 1.544 (omega) to 1.553 (epsilon); (+) 0.009. The quartz particles are typically potato-shaped sand grains covered with rounded clay particles, bentonite (131), less than 1 µm across.

Clay and water are the materials most often used to bond molding sand, but other agents are sometimes employed. These quartz grains have been uniformly coated with light to deep yellow synthetic resin. An alternative bonding agent is the clay, bentonite (131). After the mold is made with resin coated sand, it must be baked or cured. The greater cost of these methods is usually offset by the ability to cast unusual shapes since the mold once used can be broken away from the casting.

records.microscopy description: Many of the grains are covered with clay (001000).
records.Extended description: Three components make up this sample obtained near a foundry storage bin: 1. Quartz molding sand (183). Many of the grains are covered with clay (001000). This component is about 40% of the sample. 2. Bentonite (131), both free and covering some quartz grains (001000). It constitutes about 50% of the sample. 3. Transparent, rounded, deep reddish particles of hematite (223, 390, 391). The indices are 2.94 (epsilon) to 3.22 (omega); (-) 0.28. It makes up about 8% of the sample (011100).

records.microscopy description: The refractive indices of these transparent, colorless, rounded grains are 1.544 (omega) to 1.553 (epsilon); Sand grain size and shape are important in foundries. Relatively coarse grains are used for casting iron and steel;
records.Extended description: This is quartz (183). The refractive indices of these transparent, colorless, rounded grains are 1.544 (omega) to 1.553 (epsilon); (+) 0.009. The specific gravity is 2.60. Sand grain size and shape are important in foundries. Relatively coarse grains are used for casting iron and steel; finer sands are used in casting copper and aluminum alloys. Before being put to such uses, the clean sand shown here will be mixed with bentonite (131) or an organic resin, both used as binders in mold preparation.

The molding sand is now darker and appears "burned" especially in the clay coating. In addition, rounded bits of metal (100000) cling to some of the particles.

records.microscopy description: Note, however, that these particles are much smaller. This finer size is characteristic of foundry sands intended for casting nonferrous metals. Coarser grains are used for casting iron and steel.
records.Extended description: This quartz/ clay molding mixture was used to cast aluminum. Its characteristics are like those of molding sand (synthetic), used (412). records.microscopy description: Note that only portions of the grains are covered with the transparent, yellow-amber, isotropic, amorphous plastic binder.
records.Extended description: A plastic binder has been baked, or cured, on this quartz molding sand (001000). The dust is from the finished, unused mold. Note that only portions of the grains are covered with the transparent, yellow-amber, isotropic, amorphous plastic binder.

records.microscopy description: Rounded flakes (100010) of coating separated from the sand grains also appear.
records.Extended description: The sand here is like that described above, but it is difficult to see the quartz (183) grains because a dense, black, opaque layer coats all of the particles (100000). In top light, the clay coating looks like a grainy crust with very low reflectivity. Rounded flakes (100010) of coating separated from the sand grains also appear. In other places, the crust is only spotty or even dotted on the surface of the quartz grains. Superficially, this sample resembles emery (see corundum, variety emery, 218), but, of course, the relative refractive indices distinguish the two.

records.microscopy description: The variety of colors is due to varying particle size of the various oxidation states of iron.
records.Extended description: These opaque, black, rough but rounded, magnetic bits of steel (100000) are almost completely changed to red iron oxide. The transparent, deep red particles (011100) are described more fully under iron oxide (223, 390, 391). The variety of colors is due to varying particle size of the various oxidation states of iron.

records.microscopy description: Transparent, colorless to yellow, brown, green and blue-green, vitreous, smooth, equant particles of slag are 95% of this sample. Most are rounded and elongated; some look fibrous because they have trapped parallel strings of gas bubbles. Internal light scatter from these bubbles makes most of the particles appear pale milky white in top light. The strain birefringence colors are low for 5-50 µm particles. Slag particles are generally silicates including varied combinations and proportions of calcium, aluminum and iron (000100, 010100).
records.Extended description: Transparent, colorless to yellow, brown, green and blue-green, vitreous, smooth, equant particles of slag are 95% of this sample. Most are rounded and elongated; some look fibrous because they have trapped parallel strings of gas bubbles. Internal light scatter from these bubbles makes most of the particles appear pale milky white in top light. The strain birefringence colors are low for 5-50 µm particles. The indices are above 1.66. Slag particles are generally silicates including varied combinations and proportions of calcium, aluminum and iron (000100, 010100). X-ray diffraction data indicate that the composition of the major crystalline component of this mixture is Na2Ca2Si2O7. Five percent of the sample consists of opaque, black, rough, equant fragments of magnetic iron (407) (100000).

records.microscopy description: steel manufacturing dust (basic oxygen process) | About 30% of the sample consists of 5-8 µm spheres of the same compound (011100).

records.microscopy description: It is orthorhombic at room temperature and crystallizes as highly birefringent dipyramids.
records.Extended description: Sulfur is insoluble in water, slightly soluble in alcohol, benzene and ether, and soluble in carbon disulfide and toluene. It is orthorhombic at room temperature and crystallizes as highly birefringent dipyramids. The yellow color of sulfur is not apparent in microscopic crystals. Cleavage is poor, and fracture is subconchoidal to uneven. The crystals are soft (Moh 1.5-2.5) with a specific gravity of 2.07. On heating, sulfur transforms to a monoclinic phase at 98°C and melts at 112.8°C. The refractive indices at room temperature are 1.9579 (alpha), 2.0377 (beta), 2.2452 (gamma); (+) 0.2875.

records.Extended description: The identity of these opaque, smooth, shiny "silver" spheres and approximate spheres of metal is confirmed by microprobe. In its ordinary tetragonal crystal form, tin has a density of 7.31 and a melting point of 231.89°C. Gray tin is stable below room temperature and has a density of 5.75.

The indices of zincite are 2.013 (omega) to 2.029 (epsilon); (+) 0.016. It is soluble in HCl, commonly fluorescent in ultraviolet light.

records.microscopy description: Usually it is difficult to discern any form in the submicron particles. The snowball agglomerates of tiny crystals are opaque (432A) by transmitted light and white (432B) by reflected light.
records.Extended description: Because zinc oxide is used as a pigment, the particles observed are usually very small. Then, too, zinc oxide fumes from galvanizing kettles or other zinc melting operations are always very small. Usually it is difficult to discern any form in the submicron particles. Occasionally, zinc oxide fumes will be 1-5 µm skeletal crystals made up of four tetrahedrally arranged arms. In any case, they are hexagonal with indices 2.013 (omega) and 2.029 (epsilon); (+) 0.016. The snowball agglomerates of tiny crystals are opaque (432A) by transmitted light and white (432B) by reflected light.

One sees white "snowballs" and dust under top light. The indices are 2.13 (alpha) to 2.20 (gamma); (-) 0.07. Hardness is 6.51, density 5.6; melting point is 2700°C. Although the particles in this sample are colorless, they may also be brown with yellow, brown or green, green or reddish-brown and brown pleochroism along the three refractive index directions, alpha, beta and gamma, respectively.

records.microscopy description: indices of approximately 1.72 (alpha) and slightly greater than 1.74(gamma), consists of single, 2-4 µm, irregularly shaped, translucent particles. These are fused into irregularly rounded lumps with glossy surfaces which range up to 75 µm. In plane polarized light, small particles are a pale blue-green; the larger fused agglomerates are a deep green-blue with a pattern of black mottling on their surfaces. Between crossed polars, colors range from bright white in the smallest to a deep green-blue in the largest particles, which look like rosettes.
records.Extended description: This is a synthetic version of azurite often known as Blue Verditer. Indices of approximately 1.72 (alpha) and slightly greater than 1.74(gamma), consists of single, 2-4 µm, irregularly shaped, translucent particles. These are fused into irregularly rounded lumps with glossy surfaces which range up to 75 µm. In plane polarized light, small particles are a pale blue-green; the larger fused agglomerates are a deep green-blue with a pattern of black mottling on their surfaces. Between crossed polars, colors range from bright white in the smallest to a deep green-blue in the largest particles, which look like rosettes. Blue verditer is soluble in acids and ammonia and is darkened by hydrogen sulfide or sulfur fumes. It was used from about 1600 in Europe through the eighteenth century in England as a substitute for the more expensive azurite and ultramarine.

Particles appear to be soft, smearing when pressed hard, giving a duller, rust-red color.
records.Extended description: . In plane polarized light, these 0.5-2 µm, translucent particles are orange-red to red; between crossed polars, they appear to be a softly glowing red with flecks of pale gray-white. The flecks result from the image of a black cross in each particle, which can be seen at 1000X and is caused by depolarized components of light reflecting off their perfectly rounded surfaces. In reflected light, the frequent loose agglomerates are a bright, deep red. Particles appear to be soft, smearing when pressed hard, giving a duller, rust-red color. The red's density is 4.5, and it was first produced commercially in 1910.

records.microscopy description: In plane polarized light cerulean blue colors range from a grayed green-blue at 1 µm to an intense green-blue at 10 µm. A few transparent particles with n > 1.66, are visible in fused agglomerates. Between crossed polars, these 4-14 µm particles, which comprise 10-15% of the sample, have first-order white to straw yellow colors.
records.Extended description: The translucent particles of this isotropic pigment have an index of 1.84 and look like irregularly rounded to rectilinear, smooth surfaced globules. In plane polarized light, colors range from a grayed green-blue at 1 µm to an intense green-blue at 10 µm. A few transparent particles with n > 1.66, are visible in fused agglomerates. Between crossed polars, these 4-14 µm particles, which comprise 10-15% of the sample, have first-order white to straw yellow colors. In reflected light, the frequent blue agglomerates are seen to be fused. Cerulean blue is sufficiently soluble in concentrated HNO3, with heat, to give a pale blue solution. It was known in the early nineteenth century as a blue compound made by heating tin oxide with cobalt; in 1860, it was introduced as a commercial pigment.

records.microscopy description: Chrome green (cinnabar green) is a mixture of chrome yellow and Prussian blue in which the Prussian blue coats particles of chrome yellow as a surface dye. The resulting rounded, green particles have the optical properties of chrome yellow (439), q.v., and are anisotropic with a refractive index of approximately 2.4. In plane polarized light, the 0.5-1 µm particles are yellow-green and the frequent agglomerates are translucent to opaque dark yellow-green; Between crossed polars, a few bright yellow, highly birefringent, 1-2 µm particles of uncoated lead chromate may be seen.
records.Extended description: Chrome green (cinnabar green) is a mixture of chrome yellow and Prussian blue in which the Prussian blue coats particles of chrome yellow as a surface dye. The resulting rounded, green particles have the optical properties of chrome yellow (439), q.v., and are anisotropic with a refractive index of approximately 2.4. In plane polarized light, the 0.5-1 µm particles are yellow-green and the frequent agglomerates are translucent to opaque dark yellow-green; dark blue globules of Prussian blue may be present (010000). Between crossed polars, a few bright yellow, highly birefringent, 1-2 µm particles of uncoated lead chromate may be seen. Acids will dissolve the lead chromate, causing chrome green to tum blue; alkalis effect decomposition of the Prussian blue, causing chrome green to tum dark orange. This pigment was first manufactured early in the nineteenth century.

records.microscopy description: (+) 0.37±, usually are prismatic or elongated parallel. At lO00X, these translucent particles are 1 µm spheres or 1 X 2-6 µm needles.
records.Extended description: The monoclinic crystals of this pigment, with indices (Li) of 2.29 ± 0.02 (alpha), 2.36 ± 0.02 (beta) and 2.66 ± 0.02 (gamma) ; (+) 0.37±, usually are prismatic or elongated parallel. Cleavage is distinct or indistinct; fracture is small conchoidal to uneven. At lO00X, these translucent particles are 1 µm spheres or 1 X 2-6 µm needles. They are pleochroic, orange-red (a , /3) to blood red (gamma), but because they are so small, at lO00X they can barely be seen to change from bright yellow to orange. Between crossed polars, colors range from gray to bright yellow; the frequent agglomerates are dull orange-yellow. The hardness is 2.5-3, density 6.12 and melting point 844 °C. It is soluble in acids and alkali and insoluble in liquid ammonia, acetic acid and hot water. The pigment was first available commercially about 1818.

records.microscopy description: (+) 0.33, are rhombohedral, thick tabular, or prismatic with perfect prismatic cleavage and uneven subconchoidal fracture; They are rounded and have irregular surfaces. In polarized light, particles range from yellow for 1 µm particles to orange-red for 20 µm particles. In reflected light, particles are bright orange-red. Heating rounds off the particles, with sublimation at below 600°C.
records.Extended description: These hexagonal crystals, with indices (Li) of 3.14 (epsilon) and 2.81 (omega); (+) 0.33, are rhombohedral, thick tabular, or prismatic with perfect prismatic cleavage and uneven subconchoidal fracture; twinning is common. They are rounded and have irregular surfaces. In polarized light, particles range from yellow for 1 µm particles to orange-red for 20 µm particles. In reflected light, particles are bright orange-red. Vermilion, artificial HgS, occurs in a 1-8 µm range and is without the quartz (183) and calcite (133) which accompany natural cinnabar; hardness is a low 2-2.5, and the density is 8.09-8.1. It is soluble in Na2S, insoluble in HN03. Heating rounds off the particles, with sublimation at below 600°C.

records.microscopy description: In plane polarized light, the translucent to opaque particles, 0.25-1 µm in diameter, are medium blue in thinner areas to dark blue in thicker areas. Between crossed polars, much disappears, but small particles show some gray and larger particles show some pale blue. other particles are pale orange to yellow to white flecks of light.
records.Extended description: Very little morphology is evident in these very tiny particles of this anisotropic pigment whose refractive indices are greater than 1.66. In plane polarized light, the translucent to opaque particles, 0.25-1 µm in diameter, are medium blue in thinner areas to dark blue in thicker areas. Between crossed polars, much disappears, but small particles show some gray and larger particles show some pale blue. In reflected light, the frequent agglomerates are a dark blue-black; other particles are pale orange to yellow to white flecks of light. Indigo, from the organic material indigotin, is not precipitated but rather is ground directly into a fine powder. It sublimes at 300°C and decomposes at 390°C. It is soluble in chloroform, aniline and concentrated H2S04 and decomposes in concentrated HN03 to form the yellow compound, isatin. It is insoluble in water, ether, alcohol, alkali and HCI.

records.microscopy description: The 1--4 µm particles appear to be irregularly rounded; In plane polarized light, these transparent to translucent particles are colorless to white with tan to gray tones. Between crossed polars, particles are pale to bright white with some straw yellow interference colors.
records.Extended description: These crystals of the hexagonal system, with indices of 1.94 (epsilon) : 2.09 (omega) ; (-) 0.15, are thin hexagonal scales, thick tabular, or steep pyramidal and have perfect basal cleavage. The 1--4 µm particles appear to be irregularly rounded; however, at 1000X, hexagonal shapes are visible. In plane polarized light, these transparent to translucent particles are colorless to white with tan to gray tones. Between crossed polars, particles are pale to bright white with some straw yellow interference colors. The frequent agglomerates have a pale, tannish-pink cast; hardness is 3.5, specific gravity is 6.8, and it decomposes at 400°C. It is soluble in dilute HNO3 and dilute CH3COOH with effervescence if in dry pigment form.

records.microscopy description: They include irregularly rounded shapes with rough surfaces, semitabular forms, and irregular fragments. Agglomerates are common, appearing â€¢ to be fused lumps of 1 µm particles. In plane polarized light, colors range from pale greenish-yellow at 1 µm to strong lemon yellow to deep orange-yellow at 20 µm. Between crossed polars, these isotropic particles remain visible due to strain birefringence, with pale whitish-yellow to orange-yellow colors visible in their boundaries.
records.Extended description: The transparent particles of this pigment are isotropic with a refractive index of approximately 2.01-2.28. They include irregularly rounded shapes with rough surfaces, semitabular forms, and irregular fragments. Cleavage is imperfect and fracture uneven. Agglomerates are common, appearing â€¢ to be fused lumps of 1 µm particles. In plane polarized light, colors range from pale greenish-yellow at 1 µm to strong lemon yellow to deep orange-yellow at 20 µm. Between crossed polars, these isotropic particles remain visible due to strain birefringence, with pale whitish-yellow to orange-yellow colors visible in their boundaries. At l000X with a first-order red compensator, undulose extinction can be seen. The color and refractive index vary, depending on relative amounts of lead and antimony present. The specific gravity is 6.6, and it is insoluble in dilute acid. Earliest recipes for manufacture of this material date to 1758.

records.microscopy description: The crystals are irregularly rounded, rough-surfaced particles or thin fragments. In plane polarized light, particles are a transparent yellow-orange to opaque orange-brown and show strong pleochroism: (omega) nearly colorless, (epsilon) deep reddish brown.
records.Extended description: Red lead is tetragonal with indices (Li) of 2.41 (epsilon) ±0.02; 2.42 (omega); (-) 0.006. The crystals are irregularly rounded, rough-surfaced particles or thin fragments. In plane polarized light, particles are a transparent yellow-orange to opaque orange-brown and show strong pleochroism: (omega) nearly colorless, (epsilon) deep reddish brown. Between crossed polars, small crystals show anomalous first-order green and blue-green; larger crystals are often yellow to orange. Often, the crystals show a residual deep green at extinction which is usually undulose. Some quartz (183) is present in this sample. The specific gravity is 8.9-9.2, and it decomposes at 500°C. It is soluble in hot HCl and CH3COOH and insoluble in alcohol.

records.microscopy description: In plane polarized light, particles are dark orange-red with black edges, due to high contrast and strong absorption. Between crossed polars, particles are pale gray to brilliant orange-red, and the frequent agglomerates are a glowing, dark orange-red.
records.Extended description: Crystals of this anhydrous, hexagonal iron oxide (hematite) are translucent, 0.5-1 µm spheres with indices of 2.74 (epsilon); 2.95 (omega); (-) 0.21, or of 2.78 (epsilon), 3.01 (omega); (-) 0.23. Particles mined from the earth are the same as those produced by calcining goethite or by heating and oxidizing ferrous sulfate; the last are more uniform in size, and both of the first will have quartz (183), often covered with particles of red ochre. In plane polarized light, particles are dark orange-red with black edges, due to high contrast and strong absorption. Between crossed polars, particles are pale gray to brilliant orange-red, and the frequent agglomerates are a glowing, dark orange-red. Red ochre is insoluble in alkalies and dilute acids and soluble in hot concentrated acids; hardness is 5.5-6.5, and the specific gravity is 4.9-5.3.

records.microscopy description: The 1-15 µm, transparent particles have a refractive index of approximately 1.85 and are irregularly rounded with rough surfaces which are mottled with an indistinct black pattern of relief. Between crossed polars, particles having an incomplete change in crystal structure are dark orange to brown with undulose extinction. The completely transformed, isotropic particles disappear except for impurities which are sometimes present.
records.Extended description: This pigment is prepared by calcining raw sienna (447), q.v., in which process the goethite particles lose moisture, change from a biaxial to an isometric structure and from yellow-browns to deep transparent orange-browns in color. The 1-15 µm, transparent particles have a refractive index of approximately 1.85 and are irregularly rounded with rough surfaces which are mottled with an indistinct black pattern of relief. In plane polarized light, colors range from orange-yellow in thinner areas to orange-brown in the thickest areas. Between crossed polars, particles having an incomplete change in crystal structure are dark orange to brown with undulose extinction. The completely transformed, isotropic particles disappear except for impurities which are sometimes present. Samples usually have some hematite (390), q.v., and a great deal of quartz (183) present; specific gravity is 3.56.

records.microscopy description: Goethite is orthorhombic, prismatic and striated or tabular or fibrous; Most common (30%) are 9-12 µm fibrous nodular concretions which glow with a velvety orange brown. The particles cleave to give tabular, translucent 9-12 µm fragments with indices (612-620 nm) of 2.260 Na (alpha); They have irregular surfaces, brilliant yellow to orange colors and undulose extinction. Loose, porous aggregates of 1-6 µm, tannish-yellow, irregularly rounded isotropic particles with n = 2.00± to 2.15± are another component (20%). Minute 0.5 µm oval particles (15%) with n > 1.66 flicker with pale to bright first-order colors.
records.Extended description: Raw sienna consists of several types of goethite particles and hematite (390), quartz (183) and magnetite (165). Goethite is orthorhombic, prismatic and striated or tabular or fibrous; cleavage is perfect to good, fracture is uneven and brittle; the hardness is 5-5.5, and the specific gravity (crystals) is 4.28. Most common (30%) are 9-12 µm fibrous nodular concretions which glow with a velvety orange brown. These sometimes show anomalous optical effects, probably due to impurities between fibers. The particles cleave to give tabular, translucent 9-12 µm fragments with indices (612-620 nm) of 2.260 Na (alpha); 2.393 (beta); 2.398 (gamma); (-) 0.138. They have irregular surfaces, brilliant yellow to orange colors and undulose extinction. Loose, porous aggregates of 1-6 µm, tannish-yellow, irregularly rounded isotropic particles with n = 2.00± to 2.15± are another component (20%). Minute 0.5 µm oval particles (15%) with n > 1.66 flicker with pale to bright first-order colors. It is soluble in HCl and mineral acids and is practically insoluble in water or alcohol.

records.microscopy description: The colorless, transparent to translucent, tetragonal crystals are usually prismatic, often accicular, and likely to have vertical striations. In the 1 µm size range, they appear to be evenly rounded or oval. The frequent agglomerates may appear tan to gray-brown due to light scatter or opaque due to the high indices: 2. Interference colors for these 1 µm particles are low to moderate first-order.
records.Extended description: This pigment, obtained from ilmenite ore (154), is converted through calcination to a cryptocrystalline rutile form of titanium dioxide-see rutile (186). The colorless, transparent to translucent, tetragonal crystals are usually prismatic, often accicular, and likely to have vertical striations. In the 1 µm size range, they appear to be evenly rounded or oval. Twinning is common; cleavage is both distinct and poor; fracture is conchoidal to uneven. The frequent agglomerates may appear tan to gray-brown due to light scatter or opaque due to the high indices: 2. 90 (epsilon) and 2.62 (c.o); (+) 0.28. Interference colors for these 1 µm particles are low to moderate first-order. In reflected light, the pigment is white. The hardness is 6-6.5; specific gravity is 4.26; melting point is 1640°C with decomposition. The pigment was first manufactured in Norway in 1916-1919 and appears in paintings after 1920.

records.microscopy description: Particles are likely to have irregular outlines and uneven surfaces, especially in artificial ultramarine; natural ultramarine is usually more even in outline with smoother surfaces and tends to be fairly tabular. The transparent particles are medium to deep blue in transmitted light; Agglomerates are rare, occurring only with the smallest particles of artificial ultramarine which range from 0.5-5 µm in diameter.
records.Extended description: This isotropic pigment with a refractive index of 1.500 occurs often as cubes and dodecahedrons with uneven fracture. Particles are likely to have irregular outlines and uneven surfaces, especially in artificial ultramarine; natural ultramarine is usually more even in outline with smoother surfaces and tends to be fairly tabular. The transparent particles are medium to deep blue in transmitted light; in reflected light, they are fairly uniformly deep blue. Agglomerates are rare, occurring only with the smallest particles of artificial ultramarine which range from 0.5-5 µm in diameter. Artificial ultramarine should be without contaminants; natural ultramarine usually has calcite (133) and sometimes quartz (183) or clay. The hardness is 5-5.55, and the density is 2.38-2.45. It is soluble in HCl.

records.microscopy description: The amorphous particles, with n = 1.62-1.69, are irregularly shaped lumps; many are concretions of smaller particles. In plane polarized light, particles range from translucent tannish-yellow in the thinnest areas to orange-brown to opaque black-brown in the thickest areas.
records.Extended description: This pigment consists of about 90% organic material derived from lignite plus silica, alumina and iron. The amorphous particles, with n = 1.62-1.69, are irregularly shaped lumps; many are concretions of smaller particles. In plane polarized light, particles range from translucent tannish-yellow in the thinnest areas to orange-brown to opaque black-brown in the thickest areas. Between crossed polars, some low birefringence is visible, perhaps the cellulosic component of decayed plant material; silicates present have first-order white colors. Van Dyke brown is soluble in dilute sodium hydroxide to give a deep brown solution; it also dissolves in oil or varnish. When heated, tarry vapors are given off. Its specific gravity is 1.66. It was first mentioned in the early seventeenth century as Cologne earth, and later as Cassel earth.

records.microscopy description: Particles range from even, rectangular boxes with fairly smooth surfaces to sharp-edged fragments, some bladed, with irregular surfaces and from transparent in thinner areas to translucent in thicker areas. Between crossed polars, particles range from pale gray-white in thin areas to dark blue in thick areas and dispersion extinction is visible. Particles are usually 1-15 µm in diameter and, unlike azurite (189), even particles under 6 µm retain a pale blue-green color in plane polarized light.
records.Extended description: The monoclinic crystals of the pigment, neutral verdigris, with indices 1.53 (alpha) and 1.56 (gamma), may be prismatic, thick to thin tabular, or rhombohedral; cleavage is perfect to imperfect; fracture is subconchoidal Jo uneven. Particles range from even, rectangular boxes with fairly smooth surfaces to sharp-edged fragments, some bladed, with irregular surfaces and from transparent in thinner areas to translucent in thicker areas. Strong pleochroism is evident, pale sea green (gamma) to medium blue (alpha). Between crossed polars, particles range from pale gray-white in thin areas to dark blue in thick areas and dispersion extinction is visible. Particles are usually 1-15 µm in diameter and, unlike azurite (189), even particles under 6 µm retain a pale blue-green color in plane polarized light. The specific gravity is 1.882; dehydration occurs on heating to about 115°C; and at 240°C decomposition occurs. It is soluble in water, ethyl ether and glycerin.

records.microscopy description: In plane polarized light, the spheres are a pale lemon yellow and the frequent agglomerates are a darker greenish yellow. Between crossed polars, particles range from pale blue and gray to bright white or yellow; A few highly birefringent, 6 µm, white particles are present (001010).
records.Extended description: Particles of this highly birefringent pigment have refractive indices of 1.84-1.90 and are translucent, 0.5-1 µm spheres. In plane polarized light, the spheres are a pale lemon yellow and the frequent agglomerates are a darker greenish yellow. Between crossed polars, particles range from pale blue and gray to bright white or yellow; agglom-erates are pale lemon yellow. A few highly birefringent, 6 µm, white particles are present (001010). In reflected light, the agglomerates are a deeper orange-yellow. Zinc yellow is partially soluble in water, readily soluble in dilute mineral acids and CH3COOH and is not affected by alkali; the specific gravity is 3.46. When heated, it turns dirty brown. It was first discovered in Paris in 1809 but was not produced commercially until after 1850.

records.microscopy description: bakelite dust | Transparent, colorless, isotropic, amorphous plastic matrix intimately bonding round, black, opaque inclusions less than 8 µm wide, more commonly less than 1 µm. Occasionally, one finds rounded flakes of the bonding agent with relatively few inclusions; the rounded, black, opaque inclusions are also found free of the matrix (100000). Transparent, colorless rods and equant fragments of mineral matter with indices below 1.66 and low birefringence (001000).
records.Extended description: Bakelite is a line of resinous and plastic materials of somewhat different composition and application. This particular sample is both mineral- and fabric-filled. The components are: I. Transparent, colorless, isotropic, amorphous plastic matrix intimately bonding round, black, opaque inclusions less than 8 µm wide, more commonly less than 1 µm. The index of the matrix is about 1.57 (000000). Occasionally, one finds rounded flakes of the bonding agent with relatively few inclusions; the rounded, black, opaque inclusions are also found free of the matrix (100000). 2. Transparent, colorless rods and equant fragments of mineral matter with indices below 1.66 and low birefringence (001000). See feldspars (157,169,176) and quartz (183). 3. A variety of paper and both dyed and undyed textile fibers, including rayon (102) and cotton (59) (001001, 011001).

records.microscopy description: These transparent, colorless, curved, twisted fibers have a nearly circular cross section and indices of about 1.54. The fibers are birefringent and show colors up into second order.
records.Extended description: These transparent, colorless, curved, twisted fibers have a nearly circular cross section and indices of about 1.54. The fibers are birefringent and show colors up into second order. The fibers show no extinction; their sign of elongation is (+).

records.microscopy description: alpha-cellulose dust | This sample has transparent, colorless, straight, bent and twisted fibers with more or less rounded ends.
records.Extended description: Alpha-cellulose consists chiefly of cellulose but may include any other components of a pulp or other cellulosic material which resists treatment with 18% (by weight) sodium hydroxide solution. This sample has transparent, colorless, straight, bent and twisted fibers with more or less rounded ends. The fibers have low to moderate birefringence and indices of about 1.54 (001001). One's first impression is that they are short paper or cotton fibers, albeit chemically damaged, and indeed this is exactly the

records.microscopy description: cellulose acetate dust | These are transparent to translucent, colorless to gray-brown (due to light scatter), weakly birefringent, malformed, frayed fibers; Some of the particles are amorphous with frayed edges (001000, 001001). Very small particles are virtually isotropic (000001, 000000). The particle surfaces appear rounded granular.
records.Extended description: These are transparent to translucent, colorless to gray-brown (due to light scatter), weakly birefringent, malformed, frayed fibers; the indices are about 1.52 (001001). Some of the particles are amorphous with frayed edges (001000, 001001). Very small particles are virtually isotropic (000001, 000000). The particle surfaces appear rounded granular.

records.microscopy description: cellulose acetate dust | These are transparent to translucent, colorless to gray-brown (due to light scatter), weakly birefringent, malformed, frayed fibers; Some of the particles are amorphous with frayed edges (001000, 001001). Very small particles are virtually isotropic (000001, 000000). The particle surfaces appear rounded granular.

Some of the particles are amorphous with frayed edges (001000, 001001). Very small particles are virtually isotropic (000001, 000000). The particle surfaces appear rounded granular.

records.microscopy description: Cotton fibers, usually linters, are nitrated with little change in fiber morphology ("mercerization") but with major changes in polarization colors. At about 13% nitrogen, the sign of elongation reverses from (+) to (-) , hence these nearly isotropic fibers are highly nitrated. The refractive indices are raised to about 1.59 for the "isotropic" fibers.
records.Extended description: Cotton fibers, usually linters, are nitrated with little change in fiber morphology ("mercerization") but with major changes in polarization colors. The degree of nitration is determinable by the retardation of the fibers. At about 13% nitrogen, the sign of elongation reverses from (+) to (-) , hence these nearly isotropic fibers are highly nitrated. The refractive indices are raised to about 1.59 for the "isotropic" fibers.

records.microscopy description: Air bubbles are trapped in these irregular amorphous masses and sheets. The thin layers are transparent; The material is colorless to milk-white in top light with smooth-foamy surfaces and low to moderate strain birefringence (grays and white).
records.Extended description: Air bubbles are trapped in these irregular amorphous masses and sheets. The thin layers are transparent; thicker ones are translucent. The material is colorless to milk-white in top light with smooth-foamy surfaces and low to moderate strain birefringence (grays and white). It dissolves slowly in Aroclor®, Cargille 1.66 immersion liquid and most organic solvents, but it can be mounted in water or glycerin. The indices are about 1.47; specific gravity is 1.07-1.18. The plastic softens between 100 and 130°C.

records.microscopy description: This sample melts on the hot plate at 180°C (only temperature tried) and dissolves in 1.660 immersion liquid. In air or glycerin, the particles are transparent, colorless, isotropic spheres (many filled with air), flat chips and equant fragments with both rounded and sharp edges; the surfaces are smooth; In water, the sample immediately disintegrates into spheres less than 2 µm in diameter.

In air or glycerin, the particles are transparent, colorless, isotropic spheres (many filled with air), flat chips and equant fragments with both rounded and sharp edges; the surfaces are smooth; the indices are around 1.53 (000000, 000010). In water, the sample immediately disintegrates into spheres less than 2 µm in diameter.

records.microscopy description: Methyl methacrylate is a colorless, volatile liquid with a boiling point of 101.1 °C and a specific gravity of 0.94. When polymerized to form the familiar polymethyl methacrylate, its refractive index range is 1.48-1.50. The particles here are transparent, colorless and isotropic (or may be weakly strain-birefringent).
records.Extended description: Methyl methacrylate is a colorless, volatile liquid with a boiling point of 101.1 °C and a specific gravity of 0.94. When polymerized to form the familiar polymethyl methacrylate, its refractive index range is 1.48-1.50. The melting point is about 60°C; the specific gravity range is 1.17-1.20. Methyl methacrylate is soluble in ketones, alcohol, ether and chlorinated hydrocarbons. The particles here are transparent, colorless and isotropic (or may be weakly strain-birefringent).

records.microscopy description: The coating in this sample consists of fairly large (to 600 µm) opaque particles that are steel gray in top light.
records.Extended description: There is no Mylar® tape in this sample-only the coating. The coating in this sample consists of fairly large (to 600 µm) opaque particles that are steel gray in top light. At higher magnification, these are seen to consist of less than 0.5 to 2 µm, generally rounded, magnetic iron oxide particles. See iron oxide (391) for optical properties.

records.microscopy description: Some of these transparent, colorless, isotropic flat chips and equant fragments have rounded edges; others are sharp. The surfaces are smooth, and the indices are around 1.47. This sample softens on the hot plate at 180°C (only temperature tried) and dissolves in 1.66 immersion liquid;
records.Extended description: Some of these transparent, colorless, isotropic flat chips and equant fragments have rounded edges; others are sharp. The surfaces are smooth, and the indices are around 1.47. This sample softens on the hot plate at 180°C (only temperature tried) and dissolves in 1.66 immersion liquid; the sample may be mounted in glycerin. The several types of phenolic resin each behave differently in organic solvents. The behavior ranges from solubility to insolubility to gel formation. The indices vary also, e.g., those of some phenyl phenol formaldehyde resins range from 1.47 to 1.70.

records.microscopy description: These irregular polycarbonate fragments are transparent, colorless and birefringent.
records.Extended description: These irregular polycarbonate fragments are transparent, colorless and birefringent. The refractive index of the unfilled material is 1.586; 1.60 has also been reported. The specific gravity range is 1.10-1.52. The softening point is around 250°C. It is self-extinguishing when removed from a flame. Polycarbonate is soluble in aromatic and chlorinated hydrocarbons.

records.microscopy description: polymer dust (wood fiber reinforced) | This sample was collected from an operation in which a wood fiber reinforced plastic was being cut and fabricated into boxes. Many of the fibers show adhering flakes of a deep red-brown plastic (010010).
records.Extended description: This sample was collected from an operation in which a wood fiber reinforced plastic was being cut and fabricated into boxes. Most of the dust is ground coniferous wood (72) (001001). Many of the fibers show adhering flakes of a deep red-brown plastic (010010).

records.microscopy description: The transparent, colorless, polystyrene spheres in this sample range from about 25 µm to 150 µm in diameter. 95--98% are isotropic; the remainder are birefringent or contain a birefringent component.
records.Extended description: The transparent, colorless, polystyrene spheres in this sample range from about 25 µm to 150 µm in diameter. 95--98% are isotropic; the remainder are birefringent or contain a birefringent component. The refractive index range is 1.52-1.60. The specific gravity is 1.04-1.12, and the melting point is 60-80°C. Polystyrene is soluble in aromatic and chlorinated hydrocarbons.

records.microscopy description: These translucent, yellowish (due to light scatter), isotropic aggregates, generally rounded or egg-shaped, average 30 µm (20-50 µm) in diameter. The aggregates are easily broken apart, however, and are seen to be composed of individual, transparent, colorless, isotropic, smooth spheres or ovals 2 µm and less in size; The particles closely resemble petroleum refining catalysts (231-244).
records.Extended description: These translucent, yellowish (due to light scatter), isotropic aggregates, generally rounded or egg-shaped, average 30 µm (20-50 µm) in diameter. The aggregates are easily broken apart, however, and are seen to be composed of individual, transparent, colorless, isotropic, smooth spheres or ovals 2 µm and less in size; the indices are 1.50-1.55. The material melts in an Aroclor® 5442 preparation but does not dissolve in Cargille immersion liquid 1.66. It is insoluble in water, gasoline, oils and fats; soluble in low-molecular weight alcohols, esters, benzene, ketones and chlorinated hydrocarbons. Its specific gravity is 1.19 (15°C). The particles closely resemble petroleum refining catalysts (231-244).

records.microscopy description: The irregular, amorphous material here is rounded. There is some tendency to entrap air bubbles (appear opaque). The yellowish, isotropic, agglomerated particles are colorless in very small fragments;
records.Extended description: The irregular, amorphous material here is rounded. There is some tendency to entrap air bubbles (appear opaque). The yellowish, isotropic, agglomerated particles are colorless in very small fragments; much of the yellow-brown is due to light scatter. The refractive index range is 1.47-1.53. The specific gravity is 1.2-1.3. The melting point range is 218-265°C. Polyvinyl alcohol is soluble in water.

records.microscopy description: rubber dust from tire buffing | In top light, these white spongy masses show a porous, frothy surface.
records.Extended description: This dust arises from the trimming (by grinding) of automobile tires. These happen to be from white sidewall tires. The translucent, spongy masses are loosely clumped. At high magnification, 400-800X, this material is seen to be actually composed of round to oval, apparently opaque pigment particles (less than 0.5 µm) of colorless zinc oxide (432) or titanium dioxide (448) (001100) embedded in a transparent, colorless, isotropic, amorphous matrix with indices of about 1.57 (000000). In top light, these white spongy masses show a porous, frothy surface. In transmitted light, the translucent masses appear brownish due to light scatter from the tiny pigment particles.

records.microscopy description: rubber dust | These slightly elongated, spongy masses of rounded ragged outline are shaped like the macroscopic "rolls" of rubber produced by erasing operations. The surface is highly irregular and porous. If the cover slip is depressed with the side of a needle, the masses and "worms" will expand in projected area, then revert to their original shape when the pressure is removed. Although usually opaque, rubber particles may be transparent if they are gum rubber (000000) and opaque or colored if they are reinforced with carbon (black, 100000) ;
records.Extended description: These slightly elongated, spongy masses of rounded ragged outline are shaped like the macroscopic "rolls" of rubber produced by erasing operations. The surface is highly irregular and porous. If the cover slip is depressed with the side of a needle, the masses and "worms" will expand in projected area, then revert to their original shape when the pressure is removed. Although usually opaque, rubber particles may be transparent if they are gum rubber (000000) and opaque or colored if they are reinforced with carbon (black, 100000) ; zinc oxide, calcium carbonate etc. (white, 000000) ; or iron oxide (red, 010000).

records.microscopy description: At high magnification, one sees that these aggregates are composed of individual colorless particles less than 1 µm in diameter. When the sample is heated and the cover slip is depressed, the aggregates disintegrate into individual particles instead of "giving" and returning to their former shape as do other elastomers.
records.Extended description: This sample from a curing oven afterburner discharge consists of loose, white snowballs and clumps (reflected light) ; in transmitted light, these appear translucent and brownish. At high magnification, one sees that these aggregates are composed of individual colorless particles less than 1 µm in diameter. The indices are about 1.46. When the sample is heated and the cover slip is depressed, the aggregates disintegrate into individual particles instead of "giving" and returning to their former shape as do other elastomers. They could well be nearly completely ashed silicone rubber leaving a nearly pure silica ash.

records.microscopy description: Colorless, transparent particles of fluorocarbon resin. The particles are filings, and as such yield shapes which are generally elongated (001011) with frayed, fiberlike pieces (001001) protruding from the rough edges.
records.Extended description: Colorless, transparent particles of fluorocarbon resin. The particles are filings, and as such yield shapes which are generally elongated (001011) with frayed, fiberlike pieces (001001) protruding from the rough edges. In thick sections, the material is translucent. In top light, thin fragments are milky colloidal blue; in thicker sections, the fragments are milky, waxy white. The indices are low, about 1.34-1.38; the birefringence is moderately high. The density is 2.1-2.2; no melting point but chars at very high temperatures; not affected by common reagents and solvents.

records.microscopy description: The brittle, irregular flakes here consist essentially of a transparent, colorless, isotropic matrix (000000, 000010 containing individual particles and agglomerates of tiny (0.5-1 X 1-5 µm), birefringent needles and equant particles (001000,001001).

The brittle, irregular flakes here consist essentially of a transparent, colorless, isotropic matrix (000000, 000010 containing individual particles and agglomerates of tiny (0.5-1 X 1-5 µm), birefringent needles and equant particles (001000,001001). The refractive index range is 1.54-1.56. The specific gravity range is 1.42-1.52. The softening point is around 70°C; chars above 150°C. Urea formaldehyde is not soluble in common organic solvents; it decomposes in strong alkali.

records.microscopy description: The heating process has made this sample appear like 50-300 µm fused agglomerates of both birefringent and amorphous, isotropic components. The conversion of some alumina to the amorphous variety and its subsequent fusion with birefringent alumina gives the mass a mottled appearance between crossed polars. The fusion is not complete so that the edges show evidence of the 10-30 µm discrete particles. The dehydration also leaves the particles porous, which shows up as fine, elongated, dark channels.
records.Extended description: This is partly dehydrated alumina trihydrate which has a strong affinity for moisture or gases; it is used for drying gases or liquids and may be used as a catalyst. The heating process has made this sample appear like 50-300 µm fused agglomerates of both birefringent and amorphous, isotropic components. The refractive index is near or less than 1.66. The conversion of some alumina to the amorphous variety and its subsequent fusion with birefringent alumina gives the mass a mottled appearance between crossed polars. The fusion is not complete so that the edges show evidence of the 10-30 µm discrete particles. The dehydration also leaves the particles porous, which shows up as fine, elongated, dark channels.

records.microscopy description: The low relief is due to thin edges and similarity of refractive index of the mica flakes to the mounting medium (1.66).
records.Extended description: This paint extender actually consists of processed mica. The processing breaks up any "books," leaving individual thin leaves. The low relief is due to thin edges and similarity of refractive index of the mica flakes to the mounting medium (1.66). See mica (muscovite) (168) for identifying characteristics.

records.microscopy description: It is amorphous and forms colorless, isotropic, translucent, equant particles. The particles are very soft with a specific gravity of 1.01 and a melting point of 103°C;
records.Extended description: Aluminum tristearate is soluble in oil, turpentine and benzene, slightly soluble in alcohol and insoluble in water. It is amorphous and forms colorless, isotropic, translucent, equant particles. The particles are very soft with a specific gravity of 1.01 and a melting point of 103°C; the refractive index is about 1.55.

records.microscopy description: asphalt dust | Asphalt particles are irregular to amorphous globs and agglomerates of tarry material. The opaque clumps are black in both transmitted and reflected light; however, in the mounting medium, the globs dissolve into particles averaging I µm in diameter and finally go completely into solution. The particles, before melting or solution, are both smooth and rough. One reliable diagnostic feature of asphalt is that, when it melts or dissolves in an Aroclor® mount on a hot plate, the plastic mass gives off orange-brown streaks. In aqueous mounts, clumps of asphalt tend to form air pockets.
records.Extended description: Asphalt particles are irregular to amorphous globs and agglomerates of tarry material. The opaque clumps are black in both transmitted and reflected light; however, in the mounting medium, the globs dissolve into particles averaging I µm in diameter and finally go completely into solution. The asphalt is orange-brown and translucent under these conditions. The particles, before melting or solution, are both smooth and rough. One reliable diagnostic feature of asphalt is that, when it melts or dissolves in an Aroclor® mount on a hot plate, the plastic mass gives off orange-brown streaks. In aqueous mounts, clumps of asphalt tend to form air pockets. The preparation shown in photomicrograph 478B is a dry mount without Aroclor® to prevent the solubility problem shown in 478A.
