records.microscopy description: It is monoclinic and crystallizes as colorless, birefringent prisms. Extreme fibrous cleavage is apparent, and ground crystals are greatly elongated (001001). The flat laths shown in the figure show y parallel to the length and blue (annular stop) and yellow (central stop) dispersion staining colors in Aroclor®.
records.Extended description: Aspirin, acetylsalicylic acid, is soluble in acetic acid, slightly soluble in alcohol, ether and chloroform, very slightly soluble in water and in benzene. It is monoclinic and crystallizes as colorless, birefringent prisms. Extreme fibrous cleavage is apparent, and ground crystals are greatly elongated (001001). The crystals are very soft (Moh 1). The melting point is 133.5°C, and the refractive indices are 1.502 (alpha), 1.640 (beta), 1.652 (gamma); (-) 0.150. The flat laths shown in the figure show y parallel to the length and blue (annular stop) and yellow (central stop) dispersion staining colors in Aroclor®.

records.microscopy description: The product is very uniform and consists of tablets, rods, and equant or columnar particles. Most are 0.5-1 µm wide and 2-6 µm long. The transparent, colorless particles are orthorhombic with 1.6363 (alpha), 1.6373 (beta), 1.6484 (gamma);
records.Extended description: The barium sulfate in this sample is the mineral barite which has been processed as a paper filler (whitening and opacifying agent). The product is very uniform and consists of tablets, rods, and equant or columnar particles. Most are 0.5-1 µm wide and 2-6 µm long. The transparent, colorless particles are orthorhombic with 1.6363 (alpha), 1.6373 (beta), 1.6484 (gamma); (+) 0.0121; 2V = 37°. The hardness is 3-3.5, and the specific gravity is 4.5. The melting point is 1580°C.

records.microscopy description: It crystallizes in colorless, birefringent, monoclinic plates or tablets.
records.Extended description: Benzoic acid is soluble in chloroform, ether, carbon tetrachloride, acetone, methanol, benzene, carbon disulfide and Aroclor®; very slightly soluble in water. It crystallizes in colorless, birefringent, monoclinic plates or tablets. Some cleavage is apparent, but ground crystals are unevenly fractured. Benzoic acid begins to sublime at 100°C and melts at 121.4 °C. The refractive indices are 1.5815 (alpha), 1.6120 (beta), 1.6975 (gamma); (+) 0.1160. A variety of dispersion staining colors are shown in Aroclor® depending on the orientation of the crystals.

records.microscopy description: It is triclinic and crystallizes as colorless, birefringent, basal six-sided tablets (001010). Cleavage is perfect, and ground crystals are unevenly fractured, equant fragments (001000) in widely assorted sizes and shapes. The crystals are very soft (Moh 1), have rounded edges and a specific gravity of 1.48.
records.Extended description: Boric acid is soluble in water, glycerin and alcohol, slightly soluble in acetone. It is triclinic and crystallizes as colorless, birefringent, basal six-sided tablets (001010). Cleavage is perfect, and ground crystals are unevenly fractured, equant fragments (001000) in widely assorted sizes and shapes. The crystals are very soft (Moh 1), have rounded edges and a specific gravity of 1.48. Boric acid when heated to 105°C loses one molecule of water forming metaboric acid and decomposes at 185°C. The refractive indices of boric acid are 1.337 (alpha), 1.461 (beta), 1.462 (gamma) ; (-) 0.125.

records.microscopy description: The individual silica particles are much smaller than 0.5 µm, colorless, transparent, apparently rounded and apparently isotropic. The individual particles, which cannot be seen well with the light microscope, here form rounded agglomerates, 3-60+ µm.
records.Extended description: Cab-o-sil® is the trade name (Cabot) for a colloidal silica. The individual silica particles are much smaller than 0.5 µm, colorless, transparent, apparently rounded and apparently isotropic. The individual particles, which cannot be seen well with the light microscope, here form rounded agglomerates, 3-60+ µm. The product is used as a pigment, reinforcing "pigment," suspension stabilizer, to deluster paints and polymers, as a thickening and gelling aid, anticaking additive, antislip agent and as a transparent extender.

records.microscopy description: Some black coke (496) particles are also visible.
records.Extended description: Actually very little, if any, calcium carbide remains in this sample because exposure to moist air quickly converts it to the hydroxide, Ca(OHh, with release of acetylene, C2H2. The hydroxide, of course, rapidly changes to the carbonate, calcite (133). A very fresh carbide sample would show pseudocubic crystals with refractive indices above 1.75 and a birefringence of 0.05. The hydroxide has lower indices: 1.574 (omega) and 1.545 (epsilon); (-) 0.029, and calcite ranges from 1.486 (epsilon) to 1. 658 (omega) ; (-) 0.1720. The particles in this sample are gel-like aggregates of tiny, randomly oriented calcium carbonate (485) and hydroxide. Some black coke (496) particles are also visible.

records.microscopy description: They show six-sided forms differing from a cube only in the interfacial angles which are not 90°.
records.Extended description: This is a precipitated calcium carbonate and therefore better formed than a ground sample of limestone (161). Even though the cleavage of calcite (133) is very good and easily recognizable rhombohedra result from grinding, these crystals formed by precipitation are better formed. They show six-sided forms differing from a cube only in the interfacial angles which are not 90°. The twin bands parallel to the bisector of the rhomb angle usually observed with ground crystals of calcite are absent in the precipitated crystals. The birefringence is very high: 1.659 (omega) to 1.486 (epsilon) ; (-) 0.173. In Aroclor®, the omega vibration direction shows good dispersion staining colors (blue-green in Aroclor® 5442 and yellow-orange in 1260, both observed with the annular stop).

records.microscopy description: It is monoclinic and crystallizes as colorless, birefringent tablets.
records.Extended description: Calcium oxalate is soluble in acid but insoluble in water and in acetic acid. It is monoclinic and crystallizes as colorless, birefringent tablets. Ground crystals are conchoidally fractured. The crystals are soft (Moh 2.5) and have a specific gravity of 2.23. Heating drives off the water of crystallization. The refractive indices are 1.490 (alpha), 1.555 (beta), 1.650 (gamma); (+) 0.160. Dispersion staining colors are also observed in Aroclor®, but the colors with the annular stop are farther toward the red than calcite (133) colors for the same Aroclor®.

records.microscopy description: It shows no structure with the light microscope, and the particles are very small without apparent form.
records.Extended description: Calcium stearate is insoluble in water, alcohol and ether. It shows no structure with the light microscope, and the particles are very small without apparent form. The refractive indices are about 1.50, and no birefringence is evident. They are soft to pressure on the cover slip and melt on heating with some slight solubility in Aroclor®.

records.microscopy description: It crystallizes as tetragonal, colorless, weakly birefringent prisms.
records.Extended description: d-Camphor is soluble in alcohol, ether, chloroform, carbon disulfide, benzene, methanol, acetic acid and acetone, and nearly insoluble (0.1 g/100 ml) in water. It crystallizes as tetragonal, colorless, weakly birefringent prisms. The crystals are too soft and waxy to show cleavage or fracture. The specific gravity is 0.990. d-Camphor has a high vapor pressure even at room temperature and melts at 176.5°C. The refractive indices are about 1.54.

records.microscopy description: The transparent, colorless, apparently isotropic, rounded particles with a refractive index greater than 2 are mostly 0.1 to 1 µm, but some are as large as 2 µm.
records.Extended description: This product, CeO2, is used as a lens polish in the optical industry. The transparent, colorless, apparently isotropic, rounded particles with a refractive index greater than 2 are mostly 0.1 to 1 µm, but some are as large as 2 µm. The specific gravity is about 7.65. Although this sample is a lens polishing agent, finely divided cerium oxide is also used in coloring ceramics and glass.

records.microscopy description: Both isotropic and birefringent china fragments. These are 1-200 µm amorphous masses of isotropic material (000000) which also show strain and other birefringence (001000). Their surfaces show rounded irregularities characteristic of vitreous substances. Internal optical discontinuities, due to composition variation, fine cracks and entrapped gases, make the particles cloudy by reflected light and gray to tan by transmitted light.
records.Extended description: China is a vitrified ceramiclike porcelain. This sample from a commercial pottery contains two components: 2. Both isotropic and birefringent china fragments. These are 1-200 µm amorphous masses of isotropic material (000000) which also show strain and other birefringence (001000). Their surfaces show rounded irregularities characteristic of vitreous substances. Internal optical discontinuities, due to composition variation, fine cracks and entrapped gases, make the particles cloudy by reflected light and gray to tan by transmitted light.

records.microscopy description: It is triclinic and crystallizes as bluish-green, birefringent, almost equant prisms.
records.Extended description: Copper sulfate is soluble in water, less soluble in alcohol. It is triclinic and crystallizes as bluish-green, birefringent, almost equant prisms. Cleavage is imperfect, and ground crystals show conchoidal fracture. The crystals are soft (Moh 2.5) and have a specific gravity of 2.28. Copper sulfate loses water of crystallization on heating, two molecules at 45°C, two more at 110°C and the remaining molecule at 250°C; it decomposes to CuO above 400°C. The refractive indices are 1.5141 (alpha), 1.5368 (beta), 1.5435 (gamma); (-) 0.0294.

records.microscopy description: coke. Because they form the residue after the volatiles have been driven off from any carbonaceous fuel, coke particles vary in appearance. These particles from petroleum are highly reflective, smooth, black globules tending to be spherical.
records.Extended description: Because they form the residue after the volatiles have been driven off from any carbonaceous fuel, coke particles vary in appearance. Both the percentage of volatiles contained in the fuel and the amount of gas released during heating affect the way the coke will look. These particles from petroleum are highly reflective, smooth, black globules tending to be spherical.

records.microscopy description: coke (black sugar). Actually, it is an oil soot representing a degree of burning efficiency almost identical to oil soot (556), with both its foamy and brittle, vitreous particles.

records.microscopy description: coke. Black, opaque, sharply angular 30-300 µm particles with a rough, highly reflective surface (100000) are different in smaller size. These are mineral components of the original coal sample and some completely burned ash particles.

There are also some spheres about 5 µm and an occasional rounded particle to 12 µm. The loosely agglomerated, very finely divided particles are characteristic of gas burning. This gas black is from a rubber tire manufacturing company.

records.microscopy description: coke. The opaque particles in this sample are representative of coke obtained from coal. Irregularly shaped, quite porous and rough with some straight, sharp edges, they are grayblack in reflected light. They often show a fibrous structure, especially if the original coal was bituminous.
records.Extended description: This is a crushed coke sample. Black, opaque, sharply angular 30-300 µm particles with a rough, highly reflective surface (100000) are different in smaller size. Particles less than 30 µm are seen to be transparent, orange to brown and birefringent (011000), with rounded to sharply angular outlines. These are mineral components of the original coal sample and some completely burned ash particles.

records.microscopy description: coke (crystals). records.Extended description: The opaque particles in this sample are representative of coke obtained from coal. records.microscopy description: cork dust-fine | Sheets and fragments of cellular material comprise this sample. The individual cells are transparent, colorless flakes, or walls only. The rounded, polygonal cells average 10 µm across (001010, 001000); smaller fragments may appear isotropic (000010). Sheets of several layers of cells appear yellowish and translucent (011010). The cells in this sample show equant, colorless and highly birefringent calcium oxalate crystals (486).
records.Extended description: Sheets and fragments of cellular material comprise this sample. The individual cells are transparent, colorless flakes, or walls only. Birefringence is very low; the indices are about 1.53. The rounded, polygonal cells average 10 µm across (001010, 001000); smaller fragments may appear isotropic (000010). Fragments of two, three, four or more cells have jagged broken walls. Sheets of several layers of cells appear yellowish and translucent (011010). The cells in this sample show equant, colorless and highly birefringent calcium oxalate crystals (486). Their indices are 1.49 (alpha), and 1.65 (gamma); (+) 0.16. The general appearance of cork is similar to pumice (226). However, pumice has an index of 1.47 and is brittle; cork has associated colored organic tissue.

records.microscopy description: The large diatom forms are easily recognized. The individual limestone particles here are about 3 µm and characteristically rounded (001000). Ethanol may be used if necessary to precipitate out the biaxial, elongated tablets or needles with parallel extinction.
records.Extended description: The filler, or carrier, in this sample is diatomaceous earth. The large diatom forms are easily recognized. See diatoms (4) for identifying characteristics (000010, 000011, 001010, 001011, 010010, 010011). This particular diatomaceous earth is from a marine deposit. The large quantity of biologically formed limestone has the same characterizing features as calcite (133), q.v. The individual limestone particles here are about 3 µm and characteristically rounded (001000). The DDT may form radiating needles at the edge of the cover slip. Ethanol may be used if necessary to precipitate out the biaxial, elongated tablets or needles with parallel extinction. The melting point of DDT is 108-109°C (001001).

records.microscopy description: electrical contact dust | The opaque particles are rounded grains, irregular rounded fragments and large globules of metal averaging 10 µm (1-90 µm); in reflected light, the particles are silver to silver-brown. The surface appears to be made up of tiny, smooth spheres sintered into a compact mass.
records.Extended description: This dust was generated by a pelletizing machine which makes 11 % free silver-89% cadmium oxide discs for automobile electrical systems. The opaque particles are rounded grains, irregular rounded fragments and large globules of metal averaging 10 µm (1-90 µm); in reflected light, the particles are silver to silver-brown. The surface appears to be made up of tiny, smooth spheres sintered into a compact mass.

records.microscopy description: enamel dust | These transparent, colorless to tan (due to light scatter from tiny inclusions), jagged, equant fragments of isotropic, vitreous material are full of rounded, "opaque" inclusions of air, 1-2 µm in diameter. The particles in this sample average 25 µm across (5-140 µm) ; In top light, the particles appear milky-white; the matrix alone is colorless. A few of the particles may contain birefringent substances.
records.Extended description: These transparent, colorless to tan (due to light scatter from tiny inclusions), jagged, equant fragments of isotropic, vitreous material are full of rounded, "opaque" inclusions of air, 1-2 µm in diameter. The particles in this sample average 25 µm across (5-140 µm) ; the index is about 1.57. In top light, the particles appear milky-white; the matrix alone is colorless. records.microscopy description: fiber pipe dust | The dust of fiber pipe consists of asphalt and paper fibers. In a dry or aqueous mount, the particles are opaque, shiny black, irregular fragments (100000) from which paper fibers (001011) protrude. The asphalt particles at least partially dissolve in Aroclor® to an orange-brown solution; bits of the solid about 1 µm in diameter may remain dispersed throughout the preparation.
records.Extended description: The dust of fiber pipe consists of asphalt and paper fibers. In a dry or aqueous mount, the particles are opaque, shiny black, irregular fragments (100000) from which paper fibers (001011) protrude. The asphalt particles at least partially dissolve in Aroclor® to an orange-brown solution; the fibers are dispersed; bits of the solid about 1 µm in diameter may remain dispersed throughout the preparation. See asphalt dust (478) for a description of the solid and either coniferous chemical wood fibers (73) or nonconiferous chemical wood fibers (71) for a description of the paper fibers.

records.microscopy description: The aluminosilicate particles are transparent to translucent, colorless to yellowish, softly rounded agglomerates of clay particles which may be isotropic or birefringent, usually appearing isotropic with tiny, birefringent, fibrous inclusions (000000, 010000, 001000, 011000). Some agglomerates look wavy and fibrous. Individual clay particles are beyond the resolution of the light
records.Extended description: Fireclays are aluminosilicates that are able to withstand high temperatures. This sample has a small amount of limestone (133) and hematite (see iron oxide, 391) as impurities. The sample has been mixed with a small amount of quartz (183) to make a refractory clay for lining furnaces. The aluminosilicate particles are transparent to translucent, colorless to yellowish, softly rounded agglomerates of clay particles which may be isotropic or birefringent, usually appearing isotropic with tiny, birefringent, fibrous inclusions (000000, 010000, 001000, 011000). Some agglomerates look wavy and fibrous. The presence of finely divided iron oxide makes some of the agglomerates orange. Individual clay particles are beyond the resolution of the light

records.microscopy description: frit dust | This sample was to be applied to sheet steel used in agricultural equipment. The transparent, colorless to pale blue and blue-gray particles are irregular, isotropic glassy fragments (000000, 010000). They average 15 µm across (3-150 , µm); It is birefringent (gray) with indices from 1.544 (omega) to 1.553 (epsilon).
records.Extended description: A variously compounded glass that is quenched and ground, it is used as a basis for glazes and enamels. This sample was to be applied to sheet steel used in agricultural equipment. The transparent, colorless to pale blue and blue-gray particles are irregular, isotropic glassy fragments (000000, 010000). They average 15 µm across (3-150 , µm); the index is below 1.66. There is also some quartz (183) (001000) in this sample. It is birefringent (gray) with indices from 1.544 (omega) to 1.553 (epsilon).

records.microscopy description: The transparent, colorless, isotropic particles are < 0.5-3 µm, rounded (some almost spherical). None of the particles show the conchoidal fracture characteristic of ground fragments of glass.
records.Extended description: This sample is from a flint glass manufacturing furnace baghouse collector. The transparent, colorless, isotropic particles are < 0.5-3 µm, rounded (some almost spherical). None of the particles show the conchoidal fracture characteristic of ground fragments of glass. See ground glass (510).

records.microscopy description: glass dust | As one might expect, these are colorless, transparent, isotropic, equant fragments (000000) with sharp edges, smooth faces and conchoidal fracture. The index is usually between 1.52 and 1.57 for bottle glass and plate glass although some glasses have refractive indices outside this range.
records.Extended description: As one might expect, these are colorless, transparent, isotropic, equant fragments (000000) with sharp edges, smooth faces and conchoidal fracture. The index is usually between 1.52 and 1.57 for bottle glass and plate glass although some glasses have refractive indices outside this range. Borosilicate glass, for example, is about 1.47, and lead glasses may be above 1.80.

records.microscopy description: These transparent, colorless, isotropic, hollow glass spheres range from 10 µm to 800+ µm in diameter. Most appear opaque black except for a central light spot. the central spot will change in diameter as the setting of the substage diaphram is changed. Focus on the surface shows a variety of flaws and defects including striae and pinhead glass droplets. Broken fragments are flat or curved and sharp edged, with a refractive index around 1.52. the hollow glass sphere will shatter.
records.Extended description: These transparent, colorless, isotropic, hollow glass spheres range from 10 µm to 800+ µm in diameter. Most appear opaque black except for a central light spot. This is due to the refractive index difference between the entrapped gas (air) and the medium (1.66). The central spot area is an image of the substage diaphram plane; the central spot will change in diameter as the setting of the substage diaphram is changed. Focus on the surface shows a variety of flaws and defects including striae and pinhead glass droplets. Broken fragments are flat or curved and sharp edged, with a refractive index around 1.52. If there is trouble distinguishing from air bubbles in the medium, simply warm the Aroclor® and depress the cover slip: the air bubble will change dimensions; the hollow glass sphere will shatter.

records.microscopy description: These transparent, colorless, isotropic, solid glass beads have a mean diameter of 90 µm. The surface of the beads is remarkably smooth, with only an occasional bead showing a surface irregularity.
records.Extended description: These transparent, colorless, isotropic, solid glass beads have a mean diameter of 90 µm. Occasional beads have entrapped gas (air) bubbles; sometimes two or (rarely) more beads are sintered together. The refractive index is about 1.52. The surface of the beads is remarkably smooth, with only an occasional bead showing a surface irregularity. Broken fragments show characteristic conchoidal fracture. See ground glass (510). These beads are used as reflecting elements in motion picture screens and highway and other signs.

records.microscopy description: The transparent, colorless, isotropic, rounded particles are mostly 1 µm (0.5-3 µm).
records.Extended description: This particular insulator dust is of the porcelain enamel variety. The transparent, colorless, isotropic, rounded particles are mostly 1 µm (0.5-3 µm). The refractive index of most is greater than the medium (1.66), but a few are lower.

records.microscopy description: leather dust | Tiny, transparent, curved or wavy, smooth fibers and bundles and clumps of the fibers make up this sample; apparently the fibers are isotropic (000001, 010001) to very weakly birefringent (001001). The individual colorless to yellow-orange fibers are about 2-6 µm wide and average about 40 µm in length; the bundles average 10-20 µm.
records.Extended description: Tiny, transparent, curved or wavy, smooth fibers and bundles and clumps of the fibers make up this sample; apparently the fibers are isotropic (000001, 010001) to very weakly birefringent (001001). The individual colorless to yellow-orange fibers are about 2-6 µm wide and average about 40 µm in length; the bundles average 10-20 µm. The indices are around 1.54. Most of the fibers in this sample are undyed, but some have been dyed black. (They appear dark blue-green in transmitted light.)

records.microscopy description: leather buffing dust | These are mostly smooth, tangled, wavy, transparent fibers with some smooth or rough, transparent to translucent bundles of fibers. The fibers in this sample are 4 µm (2-6 µm) wide and average about 40 µm (15-200+ µm) long; the bundles are 10-20 µm (5-40 µm). In addition to the colorless undyed fibers (000001, 001001) , some have been dyed black, blue-black, orange-brown and red (010001).
records.Extended description: These are mostly smooth, tangled, wavy, transparent fibers with some smooth or rough, transparent to translucent bundles of fibers. The fibers in this sample are 4 µm (2-6 µm) wide and average about 40 µm (15-200+ µm) long; the bundles are 10-20 µm (5-40 µm). In addition to the colorless undyed fibers (000001, 001001) , some have been dyed black, blue-black, orange-brown and red (010001). The fibers have low birefringence and indices around 1.54.

records.microscopy description: lignin dust | Lignin particles are almost flakelike with irregularly rounded outlines (010010). The translucent, light yellow to orange-brown matrix (010000) has dark brown to black inclusions (less than 2 µm). The isotropic particles have a smooth to very slightly rough surface and in this sample average 12 µm (2-65 µm). The thicker particles are almost opaque, but the indices are less than 1.66.
records.Extended description: Lignin particles are almost flakelike with irregularly rounded outlines (010010). The translucent, light yellow to orange-brown matrix (010000) has dark brown to black inclusions (less than 2 µm). The isotropic particles have a smooth to very slightly rough surface and in this sample average 12 µm (2-65 µm). The thicker particles are almost opaque, but the indices are less than 1.66. Lignin is the noncarbohydrate portion of the cell wall of plant material. It is removed during chemical pulping in papermaking; it is used as a dispersing agent, as a mud additive in oil well drilling and as a source of vanillin. The high molecular weight, predominantly aromatic material contains methoxyl groups; the exact composition varies with the age, species and growing conditions of the original plant and with the method of isolation.

records.microscopy description: The mineral in this sample has been processed to a size range of <1-50+ µm; most of the blades are about 5 X 30 µm.
records.Extended description: The transparent, colorless blades and equant particles of magnesium silicate in this sample are processed mineral talc. See talc (steatite) (199) for optical properties and other identifying characteristics. The mineral in this sample has been processed to a size range of <1-50+ µm; most of the blades are about 5 X 30 µm.

records.microscopy description: The binder is transparent, amorphous and isotropic (000000). About 35% of this sample consists of oil soot from <0.5 µm rounded carbon particles to 200+ µm fluffy, lacy and brittle, vitreous particles (100000, 010001);
records.Extended description: This is a kind of hardboard made from pressed wood fibers; it is used as a building material and insulation. About 35% of this sample consists of oil soot from <0.5 µm rounded carbon particles to 200+ µm fluffy, lacy and brittle, vitreous particles (100000, 010001); cf. oil soot (556).

This is a sample of expanded or exfoliated vermiculite mica. The foliated mineral vermiculite (207), q.v. for identifying characteristics, is calcined at l750°F, at which temperature it expands at right angles to the cleavage. The volume increases as much as 16 times, and the gross color changes to a silver or gold hue. The end product is used for packing, in boards for heat, cold and sound insulation, as a filler in caulking compounds and for refractory cement and plastic mortars. This alteration product of biotite and other micas has a hardness of 1.5 and a specific gravity of 2.3.

records.microscopy description: These colorless, birefringent tablets and tapered prisms (001000) are monoclinic.
records.Extended description: These colorless, birefringent tablets and tapered prisms (001000) are monoclinic. They are soluble in water, alcohol and glycerin, very slightly soluble in ether and insoluble in benzene, chloroform and petroleum hydrocarbons. Some cleavage is apparent, but ground crystals are unevenly fractured. The specillc gravity is 1.653. Heat releases the water of crystallization. Slight sublimation occurs at 101 °C, and the anhydrous product melts at 189°C. The refractive indices are 1.422 (alpha), 1.495 (beta), 1.547 (gamma) ; (-) 0.125.

records.microscopy description: The columnar, acicular or fibrous rods in this sample average 3 .µm (1-5 µm) wide and 50 µm (8-150 µm) long; the irregular shapes average 12 µm. The surface of the rods is smooth; the irregular fragments have a rough surface.
records.Extended description: This powder is composed of transparent, colorless rods (001101) and irregular shapes (001100) of calcium carbonate. The columnar, acicular or fibrous rods in this sample average 3 .µm (1-5 µm) wide and 50 µm (8-150 µm) long; the irregular shapes average 12 µm. The surface of the rods is smooth; the irregular fragments have a rough surface. The rods have parallel extinction. The powder represents all layers of the shell. The calcium carbonate in this sample is aragonite (119) and the inverted form, calcite (133) (001000); indices of aragonite are 1.529-1.530 (alpha) to 1.685-1.686 (gamma); (-) 0.155-0.156; indices of the calcite are 1.486 (epsilon) to 1.658 (omega). Different orientations of both calcite and aragonite show dispersion staining colors in Aroclor®.

records.microscopy description: The fragments appear to be fibrous bundles like those in asbestos (120-123). the other particles are rough. The particles in this sample average 20 µm (less than 3-1000 µm).
records.Extended description: This is calcium carbonate in transparent to translucent, colorless rods, elongated chips (001101) and irregular fragments (001000) from the close-packed parallel columns of calcium carbonate in the prismatic layer of the shell. The fragments appear to be fibrous bundles like those in asbestos (120-123). The rods are smooth; the other particles are rough. The particles in this sample average 20 µm (less than 3-1000 µm). The aragonite (119) and calcite (133) forms of calcium carbonate both occur. Indices of the aragonite are 1.529-1.530 (alpha) to 1.685-1.686 (gamma); 0.155-1.156. The aragonite inverts to calcite; the indices are 1.486 (epsilon) and 1.658 (omega).

records.microscopy description: The particles in this sample average 25 µm (5-250 µm). "Pearl" buttons are made from circular blanks cut from the shells of freshwater clams. Most of this sample is from the prismatic layer of the shell; they average 80 µm (011100).
records.Extended description: These are equant to irregular, transparent, colorless, smooth and rough particles of calcium carbonate (001100); many are thin plates (001110). The particles in this sample average 25 µm (5-250 µm). "Pearl" buttons are made from circular blanks cut from the shells of freshwater clams. Most of this sample is from the prismatic layer of the shell; much is from the nacre layer; a few bits of the outside "skin" may also be found. The calcium carbonate in this sample is aragonite (119), 1.529-1.530 (alpha) to 1.685-1.686 (gamma); 0.155-0.156; however this form inverts to calcite (133), 1.486 (epsilon) to 1.658 (omega), and both are found in this sample (001000). Carborundum® crystals (215) present in this sample are from the grinding operation; they average 80 µm (011100). The photomicrograph at right shows both components, mother of pearl and Carborundum®.

records.microscopy description: The upper, whitish paint layer is about 70 µm thick. This contrasts sharply with the next orange layer (150 µm thick) which is a primer coat. These particles are inclusions in a matrix (the vehicle) which is transparent, colorless and isotropic;
records.Extended description: The layers of these paint chips are very easily delineated. The upper, whitish paint layer is about 70 µm thick. This contrasts sharply with the next orange layer (150 µm thick) which is a primer coat. Throughout the sample, individually dispersed and attached to the primer layer, is rust; see iron oxide (391). The sample came from a newly painted steel bridge from which the paint was flaking off. The paint fragments appear opaque, but, at high magnification on the thin edges and on thin fragments, the paint particles are seen to be composed of tiny (less than 1 µm), transparent, colorless or colored (both in this sample), rounded pigment particles with indices greater than 1.66 and moderate to high birefringence (001100, 011100). These particles are inclusions in a matrix (the vehicle) which is transparent, colorless and isotropic; the index is about 1.5 (000000). Top lighting (526B and C) is essential to differentiate the various layers.

records.microscopy description: paint spray dust | This sample contains opaque spheres, approximate spheres and agglomerates of spheres. Top lighting reveals that the opaque "snowballs" are white and gray globules of paint (other colors are, of course, possible) (010000) ; the surface is slightly rough. Lacquers and varnish will show transparent spheres (000000). The individual spheres in this sample average 30 µm (8-100 µm) ; the clumps average 130 µm (50-1000+ µm).

Top lighting reveals that the opaque "snowballs" are white and gray globules of paint (other colors are, of course, possible) (010000) ; the surface is slightly rough. records.microscopy description: This sample is electrostatic precipitator underflow from a Kraft recovery furnace and contains several kinds of particles: I. Agglomerates to 50 µm of waste pulp. These are made up of birefringent, cellulosic material, both fibrous and equant, mostly 1 µm and less (001000, 001011). Amorphous masses of isotropic silica. The rounded masses are made up of very minute (< 1 µm) particles (000000). Opaque black and brown and translucent brown, irregular fragments of burned pulp waste and other woody products (100000, 010000).

These are made up of birefringent, cellulosic material, both fibrous and equant, mostly 1 µm and less (001000, 001011). 2. Amorphous masses of isotropic silica. The rounded masses are made up of very minute (< 1 µm) particles (000000). These are probably from the sodium silicate used to cement corrugated board. 3. records.microscopy description: Isotropic, colorless, vitreous flakes and groupings of glassy "bubbles," hollow and randomly connected; The smooth-surfaced, isotropic "bubbles" average 18 µm (6-30 µm) (000010); groups average 40 µm (12-130 µm).
records.Extended description: Isotropic, colorless, vitreous flakes and groupings of glassy "bubbles," hollow and randomly connected; gives impression of a foamed plastic with "cells" tending to be irregular polygons; the common walls and intersections are prominent. The smooth-surfaced, isotropic "bubbles" average 18 µm (6-30 µm) (000010); groups average 40 µm (12-130 µm). The indices are about 1.47. Some fragments show some strain birefringence.

records.microscopy description: It is monoclinic and crystallizes as colorless, highly birefringent, equant prisms (001100), tablets or plates (001110).
records.Extended description: Phthalic acid is soluble in alcohol, very slightly soluble in water or ether and insoluble in chloroform. It is monoclinic and crystallizes as colorless, highly birefringent, equant prisms (001100), tablets or plates (001110). Cleavage is good. The crystals have a specific gravity of 1.59 and melt at 195°C with decomposition. The refractive indices are 1.456 (alpha), 1.696 (beta), 1.756 (gamma); (-) 0.300. A variety of dispersion staining colors are shown in Aroclor® by the various crystal orientations as the stage is rotated.

records.microscopy description: Light scattering by the surfaces in the aggregates of these fine particles makes them appear brown. The individual particles are actually transparent, colorless and acicular. The fiberlike particles have parallel extinction and positive elongation. When mixed with water, these particles quickly set to a mass of gypsum crystals with an increased volume.
records.Extended description: Plaster of Paris (gypsum plaster) is a hemihydrate of calcium sulfate made by partial dehydration of gypsum (151) at about 120°C. This causes a physical collapse of the gypsum crystal lattice with formation of finely divided crystals of the hemihydrate. Light scattering by the surfaces in the aggregates of these fine particles makes them appear brown. The individual particles are actually transparent, colorless and acicular. In top light, they are white and have a silky luster. The fiberlike particles have parallel extinction and positive elongation. Refractive indices have been variously reported at 1.55 (alpha) to 1.57 (gamma); 1.559 (alpha) to 1.583 (gamma); and 1.550 (alpha) to 1.556 (gamma). When mixed with water, these particles quickly set to a mass of gypsum crystals with an increased volume. This gypsum cement sometimes contains additions of various sorts including alum or aluminum sulfate (Keene's cement), sodium or potassium sulfate (Mack's cement) , potassium carbonate (Martin's cement) and borax (Parian cement).

records.microscopy description: Transparent, isotropic, equant, glassy particles with conchoidal fracture, sharp edges, smooth faces and an index of about 1.57. Most are colorless (000000), but many are very pale blue (010000). Transparent, colorless, isotropic, rough spheres and ovals. They average 8 µm across. Translucent, yellowish, isotropic, rough "snowballs" These agglomerates of (2) have an index of about 1.57 (010000) but contain birefringent inclusions.
records.Extended description: Besides artifacts like quartz (183), this sample contains: 1. Transparent, isotropic, equant, glassy particles with conchoidal fracture, sharp edges, smooth faces and an index of about 1.57. Most are colorless (000000), but many are very pale blue (010000). 2. Transparent, colorless, isotropic, rough spheres and ovals. Their index is about 1.57 (000000). They average 8 µm across. 3. Translucent, yellowish, isotropic, rough "snowballs" These agglomerates of (2) have an index of about 1.57 (010000) but contain birefringent inclusions.

records.microscopy description: rosin dust | Collected from the vent of a rosin crusher, these transparent, colorless, isotropic, equant fragments have rounded edges and smooth curving faces. some very large particles are pale amber.
records.Extended description: Collected from the vent of a rosin crusher, these transparent, colorless, isotropic, equant fragments have rounded edges and smooth curving faces. Many are potato-shaped; some very large particles are pale amber. The indices range from 1.49 to 1.53, depending on the type of rosin (gum or wood) and on purity. Gum rosin softens at 60-75°C, wood rosin at 59-60°C; rosins obtained as residue after the distillation of crude turpentine have softening points from 100 to 150°C. Rosins are insoluble in water, soluble in alcohol, benzene, ether and glacial acetic acid. Pumice (226) and rosin dust look somewhat alike; however, pumice is unchanged in Aroclor® below 200°C whereas rosin melts or even dissolves.

records.microscopy description: About 10% of this sample, in addition, consists of flyash: 3-12 µm spheres, slaggy particles to 15 µm and black, opaque, charred fuel. Iron oxides color many of the particles yellow and orange.
records.Extended description: This fan dust is the lightweight, expanded aggregate from shale. Like other shales, the exact composition cannot be determined microscopically. See shale (192) and oil shale (521). About 10% of this sample, in addition, consists of flyash: 3-12 µm spheres, slaggy particles to 15 µm and black, opaque, charred fuel. Iron oxides color many of the particles yellow and orange. Quartz (183) is also present in this sample.

records.microscopy description: It is hexagonal (trigonal) and crystallizes as colorless, birefringent rhombohedra;
records.Extended description: Sodium nitrate is soluble in water, slightly soluble in alcohol and glycerin, and very slightly soluble in acetone. It is hexagonal (trigonal) and crystallizes as colorless, birefringent rhombohedra; they are isomorphous with calcite (133), which they strongly resemble both morphologically and optically. Cleavage is perfectly rhombohedral, and ground crystals show irregular rhomb shapes. The crystals are soft (Moh 1.5-2) and have a specific gravity of 2.27. Sodium nitrate melts at 307°C and decomposes at 380°C. The refractive indices are 1.587 4 (omega) and 1.3361 (epsilon); (-) 0.2513. The index for crystals lying on the rhombohedral face (epsilon-prime) is 1.467.

records.microscopy description: The transparent, colorless, equant particles are hexagonal with 1.3089 (epsilon) and 1.3125 (omega) ; The particles in this sample are 1-15 µm.
records.Extended description: This material is prepared by the neutralization of fluosilicic acid with sodium carbonate or addition of sodium chloride to the acid. The transparent, colorless, equant particles are hexagonal with 1.3089 (epsilon) and 1.3125 (omega) ; (-) 0.0036. The specific gravity is 2.75. Decomposes at red heat. The particles in this sample are 1-15 µm.

records.microscopy description: It is orthorhombic and crystallizes from an aqueous solution at 50°C as colorless, birefringent plates which are dipyramidal, short prismatic or basal plates. The particles shown in this sample illustrate multiple intergrowths of two or more crystals.
records.Extended description: Sodium sulfate is soluble in water and glycerin, insoluble in alcohol. It is orthorhombic and crystallizes from an aqueous solution at 50°C as colorless, birefringent plates which are dipyramidal, short prismatic or basal plates. Basal cleavage is distinct, but ground crystals are unevenly fractured. The crystals are soft (Moh 2-3) and have a specific gravity of 2.7. Sodium sulfate transforms to phase IV at 160-180°C, to phase III at 185°C and to phase I at 241 °C. Rapid cooling to 236°C produces phase II. The refractive indices of the room temperature phase are 1.4669 (alpha), 1.4731 (beta), 1.4809 (gamma); (+) 0.0140. The particles shown in this sample illustrate multiple intergrowths of two or more crystals.

records.microscopy description: This sample consists of transparent to translucent, colorless to brown, anisotropic, equant, stringy and irregularly melted, originally amorphous sulfur, with a refractive index greater than 1.66.
records.Extended description: This sample consists of transparent to translucent, colorless to brown, anisotropic, equant, stringy and irregularly melted, originally amorphous sulfur, with a refractive index greater than 1.66. See crystalline sample of sulfur (428).

records.microscopy description: Most of the sample consists of colorless to yellow, transparent, birefringent clay (aluminum silicates) particles. Individually, the <l µm particles cannot be identified positively with the light microscope. Agglomerates in this sample are up to 120 µm. In this size, they appear opaque.
records.Extended description: This dust is from a brick company tile grinding operation. Most of the sample consists of colorless to yellow, transparent, birefringent clay (aluminum silicates) particles. Individually, the <l µm particles cannot be identified positively with the light microscope. Agglomerates in this sample are up to 120 µm. In this size, they appear opaque. In top light, they are white. There is also some quartz (183) and iron oxide (391) in this sample.

records.microscopy description: tobacco dust-coarse | One tissue is made up of heavy-walled, transparent to translucent, light yellow to orange-brown cells which are square, rectangular or rounded variations of these; These cells are commonly 15 X 15 µm to 30 X 30 µm and 30 X 40 µm (011000). Another tissue is made up of thin-walled, colorless to yellow, rectangular cells with very weak birefringence; these are commonly 30 X 150 µm (001011, 011011). Still another tissue is made up of colorless to pale yellow isotropic cells, 80 X 80 µm and some very thin cells (010010, 000010). Crystals of birefringent calcium oxalate (486) (001000) are very common;
records.Extended description: Tobacco has four major distinguishing features: 1. Cellular tissues. One tissue is made up of heavy-walled, transparent to translucent, light yellow to orange-brown cells which are square, rectangular or rounded variations of these; the birefringence is low and the indices are about 1.54. These cells are commonly 15 X 15 µm to 30 X 30 µm and 30 X 40 µm (011000). Another tissue is made up of thin-walled, colorless to yellow, rectangular cells with very weak birefringence; these are commonly 30 X 150 µm (001011, 011011). Still another tissue is made up of colorless to pale yellow isotropic cells, 80 X 80 µm and some very thin cells (010010, 000010). Crystals of birefringent calcium oxalate (486) (001000) are very common; indices are 1.49 (alpha) to 1.65 (gamma). Some cells are entirely filled with calcium oxalate; they are called crystal sand cells. 2. Pores (stomates) occur in both the upper and lower epidermal layers of the leaf; these are best seen in cross section. 3. Hairs of two kinds: nonsecretory, multicellular, branched or unbranched hairs with pointed terminal cells, and secretory glandular hairs, branched and unbranched, with glandular cells near the head. These transparent, colorless hairs are 5-10 µm wide and 50-100 µm long; they have low birefringence (001001). 4. Large colorless to light yellow spiral cells, 541B, frequently in parallel rows; they have low birefringence and are 25-50 µm in diameter. Many look like extended springs; these break into birefringent (white) fragments shaped like horseshoes, rings or short arcs (001001,011001). The refractive indices of the tissues are about 1.54. The cells with calcium oxalate and the birefringent "horseshoes" are the components most frequently seen and used to identify tobacco.

records.microscopy description: tobacco dust-fine | however, it will be noted that now the particles are so small (average 12 µm) that stomates cannot be observed in sheets of tissue, and spiral vessels are no longer in parallel rows. The most characteristic feature here is the presence of the birefringent "horseshoes," arcs and rings which have been broken from the vessels. Notice also the birefringent calcium oxalate (486) crystals (001000), both free and included in the isotropic tissue fragments.
records.Extended description: The characteristic features of this sample are exactly like those described in the previous sample, tobacco dust coarse (541); however, it will be noted that now the particles are so small (average 12 µm) that stomates cannot be observed in sheets of tissue, and spiral vessels are no longer in parallel rows. The most characteristic feature here is the presence of the birefringent "horseshoes," arcs and rings which have been broken from the vessels. Notice also the birefringent calcium oxalate (486) crystals (001000), both free and included in the isotropic tissue fragments.

records.microscopy description: Snuff is made up of ground tobacco (541, 542), hence the same identifying characteristics can be used, i.e., birefringent rings and "horseshoes," calcium oxalate (486) etc. The particles in this sample average 20 µm (3-25 µm).
records.Extended description: Snuff is made up of ground tobacco (541, 542), hence the same identifying characteristics can be used, i.e., birefringent rings and "horseshoes," calcium oxalate (486) etc. Besides ground tobacco, one finds in snuff fragments of various herbs and/or evidence of agents used for fragrance, e.g., rose, lavender, cloves, jasmine. The particles in this sample average 20 µm (3-25 µm).

records.microscopy description: tung nut (oil) dust | The important particle types include: 1. Sheets and irregular fragments of yellow to orange-brown, smooth, usually rounded bits of nut meat. The transparent to translucent, isotropic particles average 25 µm across (5-130 µm) (010010). These are hollow, curved tubes, 40-175 µm long, some with secondary and tertiary branching. They are translucent, brown and isotropic (010001). Spiral vessels, 8-20 µm wide, resembling thick, tightly wound springs.
records.Extended description: The important particle types include: 1. Sheets and irregular fragments of yellow to orange-brown, smooth, usually rounded bits of nut meat. The transparent to translucent, isotropic particles average 25 µm across (5-130 µm) (010010). 2. Vascular elements. These are hollow, curved tubes, 40-175 µm long, some with secondary and tertiary branching. They are translucent, brown and isotropic (010001). 3. Spiral vessels, 8-20 µm wide, resembling thick, tightly wound springs. The translucent, colorless structures are gray between crossed polars (001001). 4. Yellow-brown tung oil droplets, 0.5-20 µm in diameter. Richly distributed in the tissue fragments, they are, of course, characteristic (010000). 5. Calcium oxalate crystals (486) scattered throughout the sample. Their indices are 1.49 (alpha) to 1.65 (gamma) (001000).

records.microscopy description: There is no certain distinction between the two samples if one observes only a single fiber or a portion of fiber.
records.Extended description: The characteristics of this sample are those of coniferous mechanical wood fibers (72) except for two slight differences: I. This sample has fewer bundles (001000) and ray crossings; the sanding operation does a pretty good job of separating the wood into individual fibers (001011), but the fibers are very badly abraded. 2. These fibers are apt to be somewhat more yellowish than those in the papermaking sample because these have had no chemical treatment. There is no certain distinction between the two samples if one observes only a single fiber or a portion of fiber.

records.Extended description: The characteristics of this sample are those of nonconiferous mechanical wood fibers (70) except that, in general, these fibers are much shorter and are badly abraded and mutilated. Of course, when just a short portion of a single fiber is considered, there is no certain distinction between the two samples. Besides wood fibers, this sample contains transparent, isotropic, amber chips (010000) of resin torn from resin canals by the sander; the indices of these resin chips are both greater and less than those of Aroclor®.

records.microscopy description: These fibers, fiber bundles (011000, 001000) and vessel elements (001011, 011011) are like those in nonconiferous mechanical wood fibers (70) except that the bundles here are much larger than those ordinarily used for papermaking; these are 40 µm (32-320 .µm) wide and 390 µm (64-640 µm) long.
records.Extended description: These fibers, fiber bundles (011000, 001000) and vessel elements (001011, 011011) are like those in nonconiferous mechanical wood fibers (70) except that the bundles here are much larger than those ordinarily used for papermaking; these are 40 µm (32-320 .µm) wide and 390 µm (64-640 µm) long. Individual fibers and bundles in this sample tend to be somewhat more yellow to yellow-orange than those in the papermaking sample because these have had no chemical treatment of any kind to remove the lignin or bleach the fibers. Individual fibers and small bundles are indistinguishable from those in the papermaking sample.

The wood is ground but consists of more or less equant particles rather than of individual fibers. There are very few fine, single fiber fragments. The average particle size is 115 µm (45-300 J,Lm). Since wood meal of this kind is used in fur cleaning, one may occasionally find, associated with these particles, an animal fiber, e.g.
records.Extended description: The essential identifying characteristics of this sample are those of nonconiferous mechanical wood fibers (70) and coniferous mechanical wood fibers (72). The distinguishing features are the size and nature of the fiber aggregates. The wood is ground but consists of more or less equant particles rather than of individual fibers. There are very few fine, single fiber fragments. The average particle size is 115 µm (45-300 J,Lm). Both hard- and softwood appear in this sample. Since wood meal of this kind is used in fur cleaning, one may occasionally find, associated with these particles, an animal fiber, e.g. Russian sable, Alaskan red fox etc.

records.microscopy description: The thin, wide, square to rectangular sheets are almost identical to the thin sheets of wood that would be produced if sections were made on a microtome; indeed, all sections may be found in this preparation-cross, radial and tangential radial-so that in one particle the rays are seen crossing the parallel tracheids while in another the rays are seen in section (001010, 011010). Small fragments from these sheets look like isolated bits of wood fiour (548) (001011, 001010); these single, isolated small fragments are indistinguishable from similar fragments of paper, fiber, sawdust etc.
records.Extended description: This sample has all of the essential identifying characteristics of coniferous mechanical wood fibers (72). It is distinguished by thin wood sections, the results of planing or shearing. The thin, wide, square to rectangular sheets are almost identical to the thin sheets of wood that would be produced if sections were made on a microtome; indeed, all sections may be found in this preparation-cross, radial and tangential radial-so that in one particle the rays are seen crossing the parallel tracheids while in another the rays are seen in section (001010, 011010). Small fragments from these sheets look like isolated bits of wood fiour (548) (001011, 001010); these single, isolated small fragments are indistinguishable from similar fragments of paper, fiber, sawdust etc.

records.microscopy description: the edges of the flat chips are slightly rounded, the surface is smooth and the index is about 1.57 (010010).
records.Extended description: The softwood fibers in this sample are exactly like those described under coniferous mechanical wood fibers (72) (001011, 001010, 011010, 011011). In addition, however, about 15% of this sample consists of transparent, orange to brown, isotropic flakes of polymer; the edges of the flat chips are slightly rounded, the surface is smooth and the index is about 1.57 (010010). Since there is no indication of plastic impregnating the fibers, this sample must be a premix of wood fibers and resin.

records.microscopy description: This sample, collected on snow below an exhaust pipe, contains 1-120+ µm, transparent, colorless, irregularly equant particles with a refractive index rather greater than the medium. There are also a number of round and rounded, black, opaque, carbonaceous particles to 35 µm. Still other particles are the high index ones covered with carbonaceous components.
records.Extended description: This sample, collected on snow below an exhaust pipe, contains 1-120+ µm, transparent, colorless, irregularly equant particles with a refractive index rather greater than the medium. These particles are covered with iron oxide (391), giving them a ruddy, translucent to opaque appearance in transmitted light and red-orange in top light. There are also a number of round and rounded, black, opaque, carbonaceous particles to 35 µm. Still other particles are the high index ones covered with carbonaceous components.

records.microscopy description: The sample consists of 1 µm round to almost rounded carbon particles resulting from the incomplete combustion of gasoline and additives. The individual carbon particles, which may be less than 1 µm, form rounded to elongated agglomerates to 100+ µm.
records.Extended description: This is an automobile exhaust pipe sample collected on a membrane filter. The sample consists of 1 µm round to almost rounded carbon particles resulting from the incomplete combustion of gasoline and additives. The individual carbon particles, which may be less than 1 µm, form rounded to elongated agglomerates to 100+ µm.

records.microscopy description: This sample consists of irregular, black, opaque wood charcoal (100000) with agglomerates of finely divided (<1-3 µm) limestone as a filler (001000).
records.Extended description: This dust is from a burned charcoal briquette. Fuel briquettes are made from powdered coal (anthracite and/or bituminous screenings) or wood charcoal, and a filler, all pressed together with a binder. This sample consists of irregular, black, opaque wood charcoal (100000) with agglomerates of finely divided (<1-3 µm) limestone as a filler (001000). The binder in this case was a starch paste. Other samples may have a resin binder. Pitch or coal tar is sometimes used as a coating. Gypsum is another filler. The woody structure is evident in many of the charcoal fragments in this sample.

records.microscopy description: Transparent, translucent or opaque rods and fibers and branched rods and fibers. These represent the tobacco (541-543) leaves' branched vascular system with various degrees of burnings. This vascular skeleton is transparent and colorless where unburned and opaque black where charred. Even 10 µm particles show branching, not of vessels, but from remnants of attached cell walls (000001, 100001, 000000, 100000). Many transparent, colorless, microcrystalline aggregates of calcium oxalate (486) are visible in the leaf fragments (001000).
records.Extended description: 1. Transparent, translucent or opaque rods and fibers and branched rods and fibers. These represent the tobacco (541-543) leaves' branched vascular system with various degrees of burnings. This vascular skeleton is transparent and colorless where unburned and opaque black where charred. The dendritic structure remains after burning and provides a clue to the leafy origin. Even 10 µm particles show branching, not of vessels, but from remnants of attached cell walls (000001, 100001, 000000, 100000). 2. Many transparent, colorless, microcrystalline aggregates of calcium oxalate (486) are visible in the leaf fragments (001000). Many of these are found free. Burned cigarette paper also often contains fine crystals of calcium carbonate or calcium oxalate and looks much like the leaf fragments.

records.microscopy description: They are transparent, translucent or opaque, branched or unbranched rods and fibers, and tissues. Colors range from colorless to brown, gray and black. Even small particles show a kind of branching, not from vessels, but from remains of attached cell walls. Transparent, colorless, microcrystalline aggregates of calcium oxalate (486) are visible in the leaf fragments in quantities that vary with the plant species (001000).
records.Extended description: 1. Burned leaves retain much of their structural elements. They are transparent, translucent or opaque, branched or unbranched rods and fibers, and tissues. Colors range from colorless to brown, gray and black. The dendritic structure remains after burning; this sample has even retained stomates and trichomes. Even small particles show a kind of branching, not from vessels, but from remains of attached cell walls. 2. Transparent, colorless, microcrystalline aggregates of calcium oxalate (486) are visible in the leaf fragments in quantities that vary with the plant species (001000). Distinguished from cigarette ash (554) by nature of structural elements.

records.microscopy description: Oil soot "hung up" in a boiler tube continues to burn to a foamy, vitreous brown to black glass. The opaque spheres with very rough surfaces (100000) and the lacy brownish-black translucent masses (010001) indicate a long period of exposure to heat and oxidants in the boiler tubes before the soot blowing operation.
records.Extended description: Oil soot "hung up" in a boiler tube continues to burn to a foamy, vitreous brown to black glass. The opaque spheres with very rough surfaces (100000) and the lacy brownish-black translucent masses (010001) indicate a long period of exposure to heat and oxidants in the boiler tubes before the soot blowing operation.

records.microscopy description: Oil soot particles "hung up" in a boiler tube will continue to burn and eventually form a lacy black skeleton (556). The particles in this sample are black, opaque spheres having very rough, dull surfaces, indicating a soot blowing operation but not extensive attrition of burning of the particle before discharge.
records.Extended description: Oil soot particles "hung up" in a boiler tube will continue to burn and eventually form a lacy black skeleton (556). The particles in this sample are black, opaque spheres having very rough, dull surfaces, indicating a soot blowing operation but not extensive attrition of burning of the particle before discharge.

records.microscopy description: Oil soot, depending upon the amount of air present and the length of time the particle is exposed to heat, will vary in appearance. An oil droplet burning in a low oxygen atmosphere and having only a brief exposure in the boiler will be emitted as a shiny black sphere. When a sphere is "hung up" in a boiler tube, the surface will become etched, its volatiles will continue to bum off and eventually it becomes a lacy black mass (556), typical of those found after a soot blowing operation. The particles in this sample have a rough, black and opaque surface indicating a relatively short period of exposure.
records.Extended description: Oil soot, depending upon the amount of air present and the length of time the particle is exposed to heat, will vary in appearance. An oil droplet burning in a low oxygen atmosphere and having only a brief exposure in the boiler will be emitted as a shiny black sphere. When a sphere is "hung up" in a boiler tube, the surface will become etched, its volatiles will continue to bum off and eventually it becomes a lacy black mass (556), typical of those found after a soot blowing operation. The particles in this sample have a rough, black and opaque surface indicating a relatively short period of exposure.

records.microscopy description: Anthracite, or hard coal, is opaque (100000), ranging from black to brownish-black. The surfaces are smooth and highly reflective with conchoidal fracture. Pulverized anthracite coal samples usually contain some associated birefringent mineral grains (001000).
records.Extended description: Anthracite, or hard coal, is opaque (100000), ranging from black to brownish-black. The surfaces are smooth and highly reflective with conchoidal fracture. Pulverized anthracite coal samples usually contain some associated birefringent mineral grains (001000). It is differentiated from bituminous coal (560) by its greater opacity.

records.microscopy description: The surfaces are slightly rough with occasional indications of the original fibrous structure. These irregular chips (010000) have sharp edges and in places show conchoidal surface fractures. Most thin edges show considerable strain birefringence as well as occasional birefringent mineral inclusions.
records.Extended description: Bituminous, or soft, coal is translucent and reddish-brown by transmitted light if thin enough. It is brownish-black with dull to moderately high reflectivity in reflected light (100000). The surfaces are slightly rough with occasional indications of the original fibrous structure. These irregular chips (010000) have sharp edges and in places show conchoidal surface fractures. Most thin edges show considerable strain birefringence as well as occasional birefringent mineral inclusions. The refractive index varies. In this sample, it is above 1.66.

records.microscopy description: The equant particles (100000) have rough surfaces with fibrous striations and few sharp edges; In reflected light, the surfaces are brownish-black.
records.Extended description: Brown coal, formed early in the series of steps that produce coal from vegetable sources, reveals its vegetable origins in its woody structure. The equant particles (100000) have rough surfaces with fibrous striations and few sharp edges; reflectivity is low. The thin areas are translucent reddish-brown by transmitted light (010000). They show strain birefringence. In reflected light, the surfaces are brownish-black. The refractive index, which varies, is below 1.66 here.

records.microscopy description: When exposed to higher temperatures, it may also contain spherical fused particles. The refractive index ranges from about 1.52 to about 1.65 with the more strongly absorbing particles having the higher indices. The fibrous striations are still seen on some of the particles.
records.Extended description: The flyash from a domestic furnace using coal (559-561) and wood as a fuel will ordinarily contain unfused ash. When exposed to higher temperatures, it may also contain spherical fused particles. The isotropic particles of unfused ash (010000, 010001) range in color from creamy-white to yellowish-orange. They are translucent to opaque (100000) by transmitted light due to air bubbles dispersed within. The refractive index ranges from about 1.52 to about 1.65 with the more strongly absorbing particles having the higher indices. The fibrous striations are still seen on some of the particles.

records.microscopy description: This is the last in a series of six photomicrographs which show the effect of time and temperature in the boiler on the morphology of the coal particle. records.Extended description: Bagasse is that part of sugar cane that is left after the juice is extracted. It is used as a fuel, as in this sample, and in making fiberboard. records.Extended description: Hair primarily grown from the scalp of humans ( Homo sapiens ). Human hair is a cylindrical tube composed mostly of keratin . The shaft is covered with thin, flat scales and the central core often contains pigments of red, black, or brown. Commercially, human hair has often been used for wigmaking. A small amount of long, black, human hair has also been used for brushmaking.

records.Extended description: A deep red color mineral that is the primary source for copper . Cuprite is a fairly common mineral often located with malachite and azurite . Major mining areas for cuprite occur in England, Germany, France, Siberia, Australia, China, Chile, Peru, Bolivia, and the U.S. (Arizona, California). Cuprite is also formed as a corrosion product on copper and copper alloys. It has been used as a colorant to produce ruby red glass since the first and second millennia BCE. See also copper oxide red .

Soluble in water, dilute acids, ether, alcohol. Not lightfast in alkali. The original Indian yellow leaves a small amount of white ash when burned that is soluble in hydrochloric acid. Indian yellow that has been adulterated with an inorganic yellow will leave greater amounts of ash and it will be insoluble. Low birefringence. Fluoresces brightly in long wavelength UV.
records.Extended description: A yellow organic pigment produced in India from the 15th to the 20th century. Indian yellow is composed of magnesium euxanthate. It was originally made from the urine of cows fed exclusively on mango leaves ( Mangifera indica Linn. ). The washed, powdered material is a clear, golden yellow color that was popular for watercolor and tempera paints. Because the pigment was expensive, it was often adulterated with inorganic yellows, such as lead chromate . The production of Indian yellow was prohibited in 1908 because the mango leaves were harmful to the cattle. Current commercial paints labeled Indian yellow contain a synthetic coal-tar derivative that is more permanent than the original colorant. Authentic Indian yellow fluoresces a bright yellow color when lit with long wavelength ultraviolet light.

records.Extended description: Polysaccharide granules obtained from the common white potato, Solanum tuberosum . Potato starch is primarily used as a thickening agent for foods in Europe while cornstarch is more commonly use in the United States. When heated with water, potato starch forms a thick, gummy solution that becomes thinner with heating time. It thickens only slightly on cooling to forms a transparent gel that dries to a tough resilient film. Potato starch is used to size paper and textiles. It adds strength and tear resistance to paper.

records.Extended description: A deciduous beech tree, Fagus grandifolia , native to eastern North America, from Nova Scotia to Texas. Beechwood is a pale reddish-brown timber from the beech trees is a hard, tough, fine-grain wood. It is used for furniture, flooring, plywood , veneer , cooperage, shoe lasts, and tool handles.

records.Extended description: Deciduous, smooth-bark trees of the genus Fagus native to temperate regions of the northern hemisphere. Commonly known varieties are the European beech tree ( F. sylvatica ) and the American beech ( F. grandifolia ). The pale reddish-brown, close-grain beechwood is hard and heavy. It bends well, is durable under water, and gives a smooth shiny finish. Beech is a commonly used timber for flooring, cabinetry, furniture (especially bentwood chairs), veneer, plywood, tool handles, and turnery. It was used in panel paintings in western Europe. Beech nuts provide forage for game animals and yield an edible oil.

Synthetically prepared iron oxide pigment. Mars yellow is medium to deep yellow color with good tinting strength and is permanent. The industrial process for making ocher pigment was developed by the French scientist Jean-Étienne Astier in the 1780s. They are inexpensive with good-film forming properties and thus act as a driers for oil paints. Synthetic yellow iron oxides are extensively used in the paint industry to produce cream tints with titanium dioxide.

records.Extended description: A toxic yellow artist's pigment containing lead chromate sometimes mixed with lead sulfate. Lead chromate can range in shade from lemon yellow to orange depending on its particle size, hydration state, and percent lead chromate. Chrome yellow, which came on the market in early 1800s, is permanent to visible light, but can darken with exposure to UV radiation or hydrogen sulfide. Chrome yellow is used in industrial paints, some artist's paints and ceramic glazes.

records.Extended description: A bright greenish yellow pigment derived by reacting zinc oxide with potassium dichromate solutions. The color shades of zinc yellow are variable depending on the proportions of each component. Vauquelin discovered the zinc yellow in 1809, but it was not developed as an artist colorant until 1847 by Murdock. Zinc yellow is toxic, stable to light, and unaffected by hydrogen sulfide . However, it has less covering power than chrome yellow. The pure material has been used in oil and watercolors in recent years, but most zinc yellow is used in mixtures: a mixture with Prussian blue is sold as zinc chrome green and a mixture with strontium yellow and barium yellow is sold under the name lemon yellow or citron yellow . Zinc yellow has also been used as a rust inhibitor (for iron and aluminum) and as a plastic colorant. It was used extensively on aircraft by the US military, especially during the 1930s and 1940s.

records.Extended description: A permanent, yellow pigment composed of cadmium sulfide . Cadmium yellows were synthetically prepared in Germany by Friedrich Strohmeyer in 1817. The bright yellow pigments slowly began to be used as artist paints in the mid 1840s, gaining in popularity in the early 20th century. Variations in particle size and chemical composition produce as range of colors from light yellow to orange. In the 1920s, the cadmium pigments were co-precipitated with barium sulfate to form the cheaper cadmium lithopone ( cadmopone ) pigments. Another variation of cadmium yellow was a solid solution of cadmium sulfide with zinc sulfide (known as PY 35). Cadmium sulfide also occurs naturally in minor amounts in the mineral greenockite.

A thin, semitransparent, shiny paper that is strong but flexible. Glassine is made from bleached sulfite wood pulp that has been excessively beaten, hydrated then supercalendered. It is resistant to oils and greases and, when waxed or laminated, nearly impermeable to air and water. Commercially, the most common usage of glassine is for the interior packaging of breakfast cereals. Glassine has been used as a facing for the wax lining of paintings since wax will not adhere strongly to it. The translucent paper was formerly used for storage enclosures of photographic negatives, but this action has been determined inappropriate by ISO since the gelatin may attached to the glassine under humid conditions (IPI 2001). Acid-free glassine and buffered glassine tissues are available from archival suppliers. However, even this pH neutral form is not always lignin free and may degrade with time limiting shelf life to 3-5 years ( PACCIN ). In addition, high humidity can cause glassine to deform, which can affect the wrapped object (Tetreault 2017).

records.Extended description: A yellow-orange gum-resin produced by several species of Garcinia tree found in India, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam, and Ceylon. Gamboge was used as a yellow pigment as early as the 8th century in Asia and Japan. It was regularly imported to Europe in the 17th century but a few earlier deliveries may have occurred. Gamboge is composed of a yellow resinous component (70-80%; morelloflavone) and a clear water-soluble gum (20%). Gamboge is marketed in the form of dull, brownish-yellow cakes or lumps. When powdered, it has a rich golden color. Gamboge is used as a transparent colorant in glazes, varnishes, and watercolors. The carbohydrate gum acts as a natural binder. The yellow color fades when exposed to light or ozone. In some cases it has recovered its color when placed in the dark.

records.microscopy description: radial thin section of yellow birch
records.Extended description: A medium-sized deciduous tree, Betula lutea or Butela alleghaniensis , native to North America. It is most often found in the Appalachian Mountains and as far west as the Great Lakes region and north to Canada. The yellow birch produces a pale reddish-yellow wood that is tough and heavy. It is used for flooring, interior trim, millwork, veneer, furniture and paper pulp. Most wood sold as 'birch' in North America is from this tree.

records.Extended description: A banana-color yellow pigment composed of barium chromate . Barium chromate is precipitated from a barium chloride solution by the addition of potassium dichromate . Barium yellow is a fairly permanent pigment but it may turn green slowly in light. It has low tinting strength and opacity. It was not widely used as an artists pigment by itself but was sometimes mixed with strontium yellow and zinc yellow then sold under the name lemon yellow or citron yellow. It was also used for coloring glass, and ceramic glazes. Currently barium chromate is used in anticorrosion pastes and in metal primers.

records.Specimen Name: RADIAL THIN SECTION OF ALASKA CEDAR
records.microscopy description: radial thin section of alaska cedar
records.Extended description: A large, softwood tree, Chamaecyparis nootkatensis , found in the Pacific Northwest. Alaska cedar belongs to the cypress family, but is called a cedar because of its aromatic smell. The yellow wood has an even texture and a fine, straight grain. Alaska cedar is used for boat building, veneers, lumber, cabinetry, closets, and chests. It is very durable and has the advantage of being resistant to insects and rotting. Yellow cedar fibers, carefully prepared from strips of the inner bark, were woven, often mixed with wool, into blankets and cords by the Salish, Kwakiutl, and Tlingit tribes (King and Hartley 1979).

A synthetic pigment composed of lead antimonate yellow , which is produced in colors ranging from lemon yellow for the very pure pigment to darker shades. Naples yellow pigments with a greenish, pinkish orange, or reddish tinge have been produced; the color depends on the method and temperature of manufacture. It has been used as a colorant for glass, ceramic tiles, and paint for at least 3500 years. Lead antimonate yellow has been identified in objects from Egyptian, Mesopotamian, Babylonian, Greek, Roman, and Celtic cultures. In Western European art, Naples yellow has been used in majolica pottery glazes since about 1500 and in paintings dating from about 1600. It was most frequently used during the period 1750-1850 after which it was gradually replaced by other yellow pigments. Naples yellow is a synthetic pigment with the chemical formula, Pb2Sb2O7. It has a crystal structure similar to the mineral bindheimite; the naturally occurring mineral is not used as a pigment however. Since other yellowish minerals occur on Mount Vesuvius near Naples it seems plausible that this association might explain the name "Naples Yellow." There is yet no documentary or analytical evidence to support this hypothesis. The raw materials and manufacturing processes for making zalulino (another name for lead antimonate yellow) were first published in 1556 by Cipriano Piccolpasso of Castel Durante, Italy, in his treatise Le Tre Libri dell'Arte del Vasaio (The Three Books of the Potter's Art). In 1758, Giambattista Passeri published very similar recipes for the pigment giallolino. Piccolpasso's recipes call for heating a mixture of lead , antimony , lees , and salt . Scientific studies of Naples yellow include those published in France by Auguste-Denis Fougeroux de Bondaroy (1766) and Léonor Mérimée (1839) and in Switzerland by Karl Brunner (1837). Before Naples yellow came into widespread use in the 18th century, lead-tin yellow was the pigment most used by artists in Europe starting in about 1300. Lead-tin yellow was rediscovered in 1941 by Richard Jacobi of the Doerner Institut, Munich using x-ray diffraction analysis. Until then, it was not generally understood that there were at lease three distinct yellow pigments composed of lead compounds: lead antimonate yellow, lead-tin yellow type I and lead-tin yellow type II. More recently, scientists have found pigments which made of lead-antimony-tin oxide compounds. Genuine Naples yellow continued to be sold during the 20th century but the name "Naples Yellow" came to indicate a color shade that is commercially produced by mixing together other pigments, such as cadmium yellow , zinc white , and Venetian red . Naples yellow is lightfast and chemically stable, but may darken with high temperatures, or exposure to iron compounds or sulfur fumes.
